p = "docs/progress.md"
s = open(p).read()

start = s.index("| 🟨 | [#431](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/431)")
end = s.index("\n", start)
new = (
    "| ✅ | [#431](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/431) Compliance G1: data-access audit trail (the HIPAA gate) — "
    "**CLOSED 2026-08-18**, all three ACs met. ADR 0041 **phase 1** (#1318, four PRs: "
    "[#1451](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1451)/[#1454](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1454)/"
    "[#1455](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1455)/[#1457](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1457)) "
    "wired all 35 mutating routes; **phase 2** ([#1459](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1459)) added `action_class='access'` read events on REST **and** MCP, carrying **`exposed`** — "
    "whether regulated data was actually surfaced — because the HIPAA question is *who accessed PHI*, not *who opened a page*. Latency measured, not asserted: ~one commit, **O(1) in result count**. "
    "Residual split out as [#1460](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1460) (tamper-evidence — needs an external cryptographic anchor; the `REVOKE` is explicitly not one). "
    "⚠️ Proven against local Postgres incl. the production role/ownership shape; **not yet observed on the deployed stacks** | Theme 4 |"
)
s = s[:start] + new + s[end:]

start = s.index("| **Open issues** |")
end = s.index("\n", start)
new_issues = (
    "| **Open issues** | **57** open repo-wide / **39** in the **`v1.1 Backlog`** milestone, re-counted with `gh issue list --limit 200` on 2026-08-18 "
    "(the bare command defaults to 30 and had been silently truncating both numbers). Flat since the last count: "
    "[#431](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/431) closed (G1, all ACs met) against "
    "[#1460](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1460) filed — G1's tamper-evidence residual, split out rather than left implicit in a closed issue. "
    "Earlier the same session: #1318 and #435 closed, #1452 (G6) filed. The six the MCP audits filed stay open — "
    "[#1442](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1442), [#1443](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1443), "
    "[#1445](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1445), [#1446](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1446), "
    "[#1447](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1447) and [#1448](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1448). "
    "[#1419](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1419) remains open by choice. |"
)
s = s[:start] + new_issues + s[end:]

start = s.index("| **Open PRs** |")
end = s.index("\n", start)
new_prs = (
    "| **Open PRs** | **12** as of 2026-08-18 — **all Dependabot** (#1428–#1439: npm, pip, github-actions). **Zero human PRs open.** "
    "The compliance track ran end to end in one session: **eight PRs merged** ([#1451](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1451), "
    "[#1453](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1453)–[#1459](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1459)), closing "
    "**#1318** (ADR 0041 phase 1), **#435** (G5) and **#431** (G1), each carrying the mandated `/code-review` agent flow with **28 findings**, all fixed in-PR. "
    "The MCP work before it is fully merged and deployed ([#1413](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1413)–[#1427](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1427), "
    "[#1440](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1440), [#1441](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1441), "
    "[#1444](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1444), [#1449](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1449)). "
    "**Nothing from the compliance track is deployed** — see the G1 row. |"
)
s = s[:start] + new_prs + s[end:]
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("ok")

Found while verifying #310's claims for ADR [0041](../blob/main/docs/adr/0041-history-audit-strategy.md) (recorded in its Consequences).

## Problem

#541 ("every connection/user delete path has an explicit ondelete policy") was closed after the **connection** edges were settled — `suites.connection_id` via the service-level 409 guard (#753), `pipeline_runs.connection_id` → CASCADE (#724), `checks.source_connection_id` → RESTRICT + 409 (ADR 0015). The **user** edges were not: three FKs still have no `ondelete` and default to `NO ACTION`.

| Column | Parent | `models.py` |
|---|---|---|
| `connections.created_by` | `users.id` | 393 |
| `suites.created_by` | `users.id` | 617 |
| `schedules.created_by` | `users.id` | 1013 |

Every *other* user-referencing FK already has an explicit policy — `api_keys.user_id`/`sessions.user_id`/`shares.user_id` CASCADE; `check_versions.changed_by`, `connection_versions.changed_by`, `monitor_baselines.captured_by`, `assets.owner_user_id`, `incidents.acknowledged_by`/`resolved_by_user_id` SET NULL. These three are the only unset ones.

## Why it is latent, and when it stops being

v1 has **no user-delete API** (`backend/app/api/v1/users.py` has zero mutation routes), so nothing trips it today. It goes live the moment either lands:

- **#432 / G2 — GDPR Art 17 erasure.** Deleting a user who ever created a connection, suite or schedule would raise `ForeignKeyViolation` → unhandled 500, exactly the #540/#724 shape.
- **ADR 0041 phase 1 (#1318)**, whose `actor_user_id` is deliberately `SET NULL` with a denormalized `actor_label` so attribution survives a user delete — which only helps if the user delete can happen at all.

Filed rather than left in prose per CONTRIBUTING rule 3a: "pre-existing" is not a disposition, and this one is pre-existing *and* pre-scheduled to bite.

## Decision needed

`SET NULL` (a suite outlives its author, matching every `changed_by`/`owner_user_id` precedent) vs. RESTRICT-with-409 (matching the connection-delete guard). `SET NULL` is the obvious fit — `created_by` is provenance, not ownership-of-lifecycle, and blocking a user's erasure on a suite they created is the wrong answer for #432 — but the columns are currently `NOT NULL` on at least `suites.created_by`/`connections.created_by`, so `SET NULL` needs a nullable widen first (two-step per CONTRIBUTING rule 30).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Policy decided and recorded per edge; columns widened to nullable where `SET NULL` is chosen (separate, backward-compatible migration step)
- [ ] Alembic migration(s) apply the `ondelete`; up + down tested locally
- [ ] Regression test: delete a user who created a connection, a suite and a schedule → no 500, children behave as decided
- [ ] Re-audit: `grep 'ForeignKey' backend/app/db/models.py | grep -v ondelete` returns nothing unexplained, and the result is asserted by a test so the next new FK cannot silently reintroduce the gap

"""created_by: nullable + ON DELETE SET NULL on the three user FKs (#1319)

`connections.created_by`, `suites.created_by` and `schedules.created_by` were the
only user-referencing foreign keys with no `ondelete` policy, so they defaulted to
`NO ACTION`. Every other one already has an explicit policy — `api_keys.user_id`
/ `sessions.user_id` / `shares.user_id` CASCADE; `changed_by`, `owner_user_id`,
`acknowledged_by`, `resolved_by_user_id` and `audit_events.actor_user_id` SET
NULL.

**`SET NULL`, not RESTRICT.** `created_by` is *provenance* — who made this — not
ownership of the row's lifecycle. RESTRICT would make a user un-erasable because
they once created a suite, which is the wrong answer for GDPR Art 17 erasure
(#432), the very feature this unblocks. It also matches the ADR-0041 shape
already in place next door: `audit_events.actor_user_id` is SET NULL with a
denormalized `actor_label`, so attribution survives the delete — which only helps
if the delete can happen at all.

**Why nullable and the FK change ship together, and why that is
backward-compatible.** `SET NULL` requires the column to be nullable, and the two
must be consistent: a nullable column with a `NO ACTION` FK is the same latent
500, and a `SET NULL` FK on a NOT NULL column would fail at delete time instead.
Shipping them apart would leave a window in which one of those states is live.

The pair is safe to deploy in one step because **no NULL can appear before the
new code is running**: there is no user-delete route anywhere in the app
(`api/v1/users.py` has zero mutation routes), so the only producer of a NULL
`created_by` is a cascade that cannot be triggered yet. Code deployed *before*
this migration keeps working unmodified — it writes a non-null value, which a
nullable column accepts — and code deployed *after* tolerates the NULL it still
cannot yet observe. That is the CONTRIBUTING two-step ordering satisfied by the
absence of a producer rather than by splitting the change; recorded here because
"it's just a widen" is exactly the reasoning that gets this wrong.

Widening NOT NULL → NULL is a catalog-only change on Postgres (no table rewrite,
no scan). Dropping and recreating a foreign key takes a brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
lock on the child table and re-validates it, which is a scan of the child — all
three are small tables (connections, suites, schedules), so this is cheap; on a
large child table it would not be.

Tested up + down locally against real Postgres, including with rows present.
Rollback: `downgrade()` restores NOT NULL and the policy-less FK. It **fails
loudly if any row has a NULL `created_by`**, which is correct — those rows exist
precisely because a user was erased, and inventing an author for them would be
worse than refusing.

they once created a suite, which is the wrong answer for GDPR Art 17 erasure

backward-compatible.** `SET NULL` requires the column to be nullable, and the two
must be consistent: a nullable column with a `NO ACTION` FK is the same latent

absence of a producer rather than by splitting the change; recorded here because
"it's just a widen" is exactly the reasoning that gets this wrong.

Widening NOT NULL → NULL is a catalog-only change on Postgres (no table rewrite,

"""Every foreign key must state an `ondelete` policy — #1319, #541.

#541 was closed after the *connection* edges were settled, and the **user** edges
were missed: three `created_by` FKs still defaulted to `NO ACTION`, which is a
latent unhandled 500 the moment a user-delete path exists (GDPR Art 17 erasure,
#432). It was found by hand while verifying something else. This test is why that
cannot happen a third time.

**It enumerates the real metadata**, so a foreign key added tomorrow appears here
whether or not its author knew the rule — the ADR-0039 lesson about guards that
iterate their own registrations.

`NO ACTION` is not banned outright; it is banned *silently*. An edge that
genuinely wants it declares itself in `_EXPLICIT_NO_ACTION` with the reason,
because "the delete is refused at the service layer" is a real answer and an
unexplained default is not distinguishable from an oversight.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Final

from backend.app.db.models import Base

#: Edges deliberately left without a database-level `ondelete`, each with the
#: mechanism that handles the delete instead. A path, not a pattern — adding one
#: is a decision a reviewer can read.
_EXPLICIT_NO_ACTION: Final[dict[str, str]] = {
    "suites.connection_id": (
        "guarded at the service layer with a 409 while any suite runs against the "
        "connection (#753). A database policy here would be wrong in both "
        "directions: CASCADE would silently destroy suites (and their runs and "
        "results, #540) with a connection, and SET NULL would leave a suite that "
        "can never run and cannot say why."
    ),
}


def _edges_without_ondelete() -> dict[str, str]:
    """`table.column` → referenced table, for every FK with no `ondelete`."""
    found: dict[str, str] = {}
    for table in Base.metadata.sorted_tables:
        for column in table.columns:
            for fk in column.foreign_keys:
                if fk.ondelete is None:
                    found[f"{table.name}.{column.name}"] = fk.target_fullname
    return found


def test_the_scan_sees_the_real_schema() -> None:
    """The guard's own guard: every assertion below is vacuously true against an
    empty metadata, so the enumeration is checked before it is trusted."""
    total = sum(
        1 for t in Base.metadata.sorted_tables for c in t.columns for _ in c.foreign_keys
    )
    assert total > 20, f"only {total} foreign keys found — the scan is not seeing the schema"


def test_every_foreign_key_declares_an_ondelete_policy() -> None:
    """A new FK must choose a policy or justify not having one."""
    undeclared = {
        edge: target
        for edge, target in _edges_without_ondelete().items()
        if edge not in _EXPLICIT_NO_ACTION
    }
    assert not undeclared, (
        f"these foreign keys have no `ondelete` and default to NO ACTION: {undeclared} — "
        "a delete of the parent will raise ForeignKeyViolation and surface as an "
        "unhandled 500. Choose CASCADE / SET NULL / RESTRICT on the column, or add the "
        "edge to _EXPLICIT_NO_ACTION with the service-layer mechanism that handles it "
        "instead. #1319."
    )


def test_the_exemption_list_carries_no_edges_that_now_have_a_policy() -> None:
    """A stale exemption is worse than a missing one: it documents a mechanism
    that may no longer exist, while the edge quietly behaves differently."""
    stale = set(_EXPLICIT_NO_ACTION) - set(_edges_without_ondelete())
    assert not stale, (
        f"these edges now declare an `ondelete` and no longer need an exemption: "
        f"{sorted(stale)} — remove them from _EXPLICIT_NO_ACTION"
    )


def test_every_exemption_states_its_mechanism() -> None:
    """An unexplained exemption is indistinguishable from the oversight this test
    exists to catch."""
    thin = {edge: why for edge, why in _EXPLICIT_NO_ACTION.items() if len(why.strip()) < 40}
    assert not thin, f"exemptions with no substantive mechanism: {sorted(thin)}"


def test_the_user_provenance_edges_are_set_null() -> None:
    """The three edges #1319 is about, asserted by name.

    Named rather than left to the general rule because *which* policy they carry
    is the decision, not merely that they carry one: `created_by` is provenance,
    so the row outlives its author. RESTRICT would satisfy the rule above and be
    wrong — it would make a user un-erasable because they once created a suite,
    which is the opposite of what GDPR Art 17 (#432) needs.
    """
    for table_name, column_name in (
        ("connections", "created_by"),
        ("suites", "created_by"),
        ("schedules", "created_by"),
    ):
        column = Base.metadata.tables[table_name].columns[column_name]
        fk = next(iter(column.foreign_keys))
        assert fk.ondelete == "SET NULL", f"{table_name}.{column_name} is {fk.ondelete}"
        assert column.nullable, (
            f"{table_name}.{column_name} is NOT NULL, so SET NULL would fail at "
            "delete time — the two must agree"
        )

"""Deleting a user must not 500 — #1319, and the prerequisite for #432 erasure.

Three `created_by` foreign keys defaulted to `NO ACTION`, so deleting a user who
had ever created a connection, a suite or a schedule raised `ForeignKeyViolation`.
Latent only because v1 has no user-delete route at all; GDPR Art 17 erasure (#432)
is what makes it live.

Exercised through the ORM against real Postgres rather than by reading the model,
because `ondelete` is enforced by the **database** — a model attribute asserts
what we declared, and only a delete asserts what happens.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import uuid
from typing import Any

from backend.app.db.models import Connection, Schedule, Suite, User


def test_deleting_a_user_nulls_provenance_and_keeps_the_rows(db_session: Any) -> None:
    """The children survive with `created_by` NULL.

    Survival is the point, and it is the half a test could easily get wrong by
    asserting only "no exception": CASCADE would also raise nothing, while
    silently destroying every connection, suite and schedule the departing user
    ever made — for a leaver in a real workspace, that is most of it.
    """
    author = User(aad_object_id=uuid.uuid4().hex, email=f"a-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}@example.com")
    db_session.add(author)
    db_session.flush()

    conn = Connection(
        name=f"c-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}",
        type="snowflake",
        env="dev",
        config={"account": "x"},
        created_by=author.id,
    )

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
fix(db): created_by → nullable + ON DELETE SET NULL on the three user FKs (#1319)

`connections.created_by`, `suites.created_by` and `schedules.created_by` were the
only user-referencing foreign keys with no `ondelete`, so they defaulted to NO
ACTION. Deleting a user who had ever created any of the three raised
ForeignKeyViolation — an unhandled 500. Latent only because v1 has no user-delete
route at all; GDPR Art 17 erasure (#432) is what makes it live, and this unblocks
it.

**SET NULL, not RESTRICT.** `created_by` is provenance — who made this — not
ownership of the row's lifecycle. RESTRICT would make a user un-erasable because
they once created a suite, which is the wrong answer for the very feature this
unblocks, and it matches the shape already next door: `audit_events.actor_user_id`
is SET NULL with a denormalized label so attribution survives the delete — which
only helps if the delete can happen at all.

The nullable widen and the FK change ship together, and the reason is written into
the migration rather than assumed: the two must be consistent (a nullable column
with a NO ACTION FK is the same latent 500; a SET NULL FK on a NOT NULL column
fails at delete time), and no NULL can appear before the new code runs because
there is no user-delete route to produce one. That satisfies the two-step ordering
by the absence of a producer, not by splitting the change.

Verified against real Postgres rather than by reading the model, because
`ondelete` is enforced by the DATABASE:

* migration up, down and up again on a clean database;
* seeded a user with a connection, a suite and a schedule, deleted the user —
  `DELETE 1`, all three rows survive with `created_by` NULL (`confdeltype = n` on
  all three constraints);
* downgrade with a NULL present REFUSES with NotNullViolation, which is correct:
  those rows exist because a user was erased, and inventing an author would be
  worse than refusing. Documented as intended behaviour, not a rough edge.

Two guards, both mutation-checked. `test_fk_ondelete_policy` enumerates the real
metadata so a foreign key added tomorrow appears whether or not its author knew
the rule (#541 was closed with these three still open, found by hand); NO ACTION
is not banned, only banned SILENTLY — `suites.connection_id` declares itself with
the 409 mechanism that handles it instead. And an end-to-end delete test asserts
the children SURVIVE, which is the half a naive test misses: CASCADE also raises
nothing while silently destroying every connection, suite and schedule a departing
user ever made. The CASCADE mutation kills three tests.

The type change rippled into six test call sites that relied on non-nullability —
narrowed rather than cast blindly, so a real None fails in the test instead of
inside the service. Two API response models widened to `uuid.UUID | None`; a
non-optional field would 500 on serialization once a NULL exists.

Full suite 4737 passed. Black / Ruff / mypy / Bandit clean.

Closes #1319. Unblocks #432.

gh pr create --title "fix(db): created_by → nullable + ON DELETE SET NULL on the three user FKs (#1319)" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
The last unblocked prerequisite for **G2 / GDPR Art 17 erasure** ([#432](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/432)).

`connections.created_by`, `suites.created_by` and `schedules.created_by` were the **only** user-referencing foreign keys with no `ondelete`, so they defaulted to `NO ACTION`. Deleting a user who had ever created any of the three raised `ForeignKeyViolation` — an unhandled 500. Latent only because v1 has no user-delete route at all.

## SET NULL, not RESTRICT

`created_by` is **provenance** — who made this — not ownership of the row's lifecycle. RESTRICT would make a user un-erasable because they once created a suite, which is the wrong answer for the very feature this unblocks. It also matches the shape already next door: `audit_events.actor_user_id` is SET NULL with a denormalized `actor_label` so attribution survives the delete — which only helps if the delete can happen at all.

## Why the widen and the FK change ship together

Written into the migration rather than assumed. They **must** be consistent — a nullable column with a `NO ACTION` FK is the same latent 500, and a `SET NULL` FK on a `NOT NULL` column fails at delete time — and **no NULL can appear before the new code runs**, because there is no user-delete route to produce one. That satisfies the two-step ordering by the *absence of a producer*, not by splitting the change.

## Verified against real Postgres, not by reading the model

`ondelete` is enforced by the **database**, so a model attribute asserts what we declared and only a delete asserts what happens:

- migration up → down → up on a clean database;
- seeded a user with a connection, a suite and a schedule, deleted the user → **`DELETE 1`**, all three rows survive with `created_by` NULL (`confdeltype = n` on all three constraints);
- **downgrade with a NULL present REFUSES** with `NotNullViolation` — correct, and documented as intended: those rows exist *because* a user was erased, so inventing an author would be worse than refusing.

## Two guards, both mutation-checked

**`test_fk_ondelete_policy`** enumerates the real metadata, so a foreign key added tomorrow appears whether or not its author knew the rule. That matters here specifically: **#541 was closed with these three still open**, and they were found by hand while verifying something unrelated. `NO ACTION` is not banned outright — only banned *silently*; `suites.connection_id` declares itself with the 409 mechanism (#753) that handles it instead.

**The end-to-end delete test asserts the children SURVIVE**, which is the half a naive test misses: CASCADE also raises nothing, while silently destroying every connection, suite and schedule a departing user ever made — for a leaver in a real workspace, most of it. The CASCADE mutation kills three tests.

A second test pins the authz consequence: an authorless suite grants **nobody** ownership. `suite_authz` compares `suite.created_by == user_id`, and the unsafe direction is a one-character difference that would hand every user ownership of every suite whose author was erased.

## Ripple

The type change surfaced six test call sites relying on non-nullability — **narrowed rather than cast blindly**, so a real `None` fails in the test instead of inside the service. Two API response models widened to `uuid.UUID | None`; a non-optional field would 500 on serialization once a NULL exists.

Full suite **4737 passed**. Black / Ruff / mypy / Bandit clean.

Closes #1319. Unblocks #432.

def test_an_ownerless_suite_stays_visible_in_the_admin_overview(db_session: Any) -> None:
    """The consequence one PR over, and the reason it matters more than it looks.

    `list_all_suites` inner-joined the author, so a suite whose creator was erased
    dropped out of the Admin control centre **entirely** — while still running on
    its schedules and still holding its shares. Invisible and active is the worst
    combination available: an admin reviewing the workspace would not see the one
    suite with nobody obviously responsible for it.

    Found by review, on a file this change never touched — a widened column ages
    every query that assumed it was NOT NULL.
    """
    from backend.app.services import admin_service

    author = User(aad_object_id=uuid.uuid4().hex, email=f"a-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}@example.com")
    db_session.add(author)
    db_session.flush()
    conn = Connection(
        name=f"c-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}",
        type="snowflake",
        env="dev",
        config={"account": "x"},
        created_by=author.id,
    )
    db_session.add(conn)
    db_session.flush()
    suite = Suite(name=f"orphan-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:6]}", connection_id=conn.id, created_by=author.id)
    db_session.add(suite)
    db_session.commit()
    suite_id, suite_name = suite.id, suite.name

    assert any(r.id == suite_id for r in admin_service.list_all_suites(db_session)), (
        "precondition: the suite is listed while its author exists"
    )

    db_session.delete(author)
    db_session.commit()
    db_session.expire_all()

    listed = {r.id: r for r in admin_service.list_all_suites(db_session)}
    assert suite_id in listed, (
        f"the suite {suite_name!r} vanished from the admin overview when its author "
        "was erased — it still runs, so it must still be visible"
    )
    row = listed[suite_id]
    assert row.owner_id is None and row.owner_email is None, (
        "an erased author must read as absent, not as a stale or invented owner"
    )

    """`list_all_access` is the other side, and it wants the OPPOSITE handling.

    There, an erased author leaves no grant to report — a row with a null user
    would render as a grant to nobody. Its absence is correct here, while its
    absence from the suites overview above is not, which is exactly why the two
    joins treat the null differently. Asserted so that "make them consistent"

        type="snowflake",
        env="dev",
        config={"account": "x"},
        created_by=author.id,
    )
    db_session.add(conn)
    db_session.flush()
    suite = Suite(name=f"s-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}", connection_id=conn.id, created_by=author.id)
    db_session.add(suite)
    db_session.commit()
    suite_id = suite.id

    db_session.delete(author)
    db_session.commit()
    db_session.expire_all()

Reviewed PR #1463 (`feat(redaction): fail-closed column policy — G3 half`). 5 findings, all posted as inline comments.

**Findings**

- `backend/app/api/v1/suites.py:640` — PUT `/column-policy` is full-replacement and `require_classification` defaults to `False`, so the shipped frontend (`SamplePolicyPanel.onSave` / `columnPolicy.ts` send only `identifier_column` + `pii_columns`) silently disables fail-closed mode on any Save. **High.**
- `backend/app/services/suite_service.py:248` — the new defaulted kwarg means pre-existing callers drop the flag; the MCP `set_column_policy` tool clears it, and MCP `get_column_policy` doesn't return it, so the read-modify-write its docstring prescribes cannot preserve it. **High.**
- `backend/app/services/run_service.py:1107` — in fail-closed mode `_known_sensitive` clears the identifier column without consulting `is_sensitive`, so an `identifier_column` holding emails is *shown* in fail-closed and *masked* in default mode. The mode can loosen, contradicting both the sibling docstring and `docs/compliance-posture.md`. **High.**
- `backend/app/services/run_service.py:1135` — `_may_show_incidental`'s fail-closed branch returns True on a non-sensitive tag with no classifier check, so (once tags are populated) a `public`-tagged EMAIL column is shown in fail-closed but masked by default. **Medium.**
- `backend/app/services/run_service.py:1056` — `_NON_SENSITIVE_TAG_VALUES` includes `internal`, a confidentiality *level* (and the common default stamp), not an assertion of non-personal data; it would clear whole tables. **Medium.**

The precedence-matrix tests and the fail-closed unit tests themselves look sound — they cover the tightening direction; what's untested is the loosening direction (identifier/tag clearance vs. `is_sensitive`) and the API round-trip/preservation of the flag.

        # looks harmless is exactly what this mode refuses to act on.
        #
        # **A clearance still does not beat an affirmative PII signal.** An
        # earlier version returned on the clearance alone, which made this mode
        # LOOSEN: an `identifier_column` holding emails was shown in fail-closed
        # and masked in default mode. A mode whose whole promise is "tighter"
        # must never be the reason something is surfaced, so the affirmative test
        # still runs — the mode removes the permissive fallback, not the floor.
        cleared = _tag_non_sensitive(column, tags) or _policy_identifier(column, policy)
        if not cleared:

        return is_sensitive(column, values, value_signal_summary=value_signal_summary)"""
assert old in s

        # clearance. Note the identifier still passes `is_sensitive` below — a

new = """    if _policy_requires_classification(policy):

        if not (_tag_non_sensitive(column, tags) or _policy_identifier(column, policy)):

def test_a_policy_save_without_the_flag_does_not_disable_fail_closed(
    client: TestClient, db_session: Any
) -> None:
    """The highest-severity finding on #1463: a security control that turns itself
    off.

    `PUT /column-policy` is a full replacement, and every client that predates the
    flag — including our own shipped Save button and the MCP `set_column_policy`
    tool — sends the policy WITHOUT it. With a plain `False` default, editing an
    unrelated field silently switched fail-closed off, on a suite chosen for
    fail-closed precisely because its data is regulated.

    Absence therefore preserves. Turning it off stays possible; it just has to be
    said out loud, which the second half asserts so "preserve" cannot quietly
    become "immutable".
    """
    sid = _make_suite(client)

    enabled = client.put(
        f"/api/v1/suites/{sid}/column-policy",
        json={"identifier_column": "ORDER_ID", "pii_columns": ["EMAIL"], "require_classification": True},
    )
    assert enabled.status_code == 200
    assert enabled.json()["require_classification"] is True

    # A pre-flag client's Save: identifier + pii only.
    resaved = client.put(
        f"/api/v1/suites/{sid}/column-policy",
        json={"identifier_column": "ORDER_ID", "pii_columns": ["EMAIL", "PHONE"]},
    )
    assert resaved.status_code == 200
    assert resaved.json()["pii_columns"] == ["EMAIL", "PHONE"], "the edit still applies"
    assert resaved.json()["require_classification"] is True, (

    # …and an explicit false still turns it off.
    disabled = client.put(
        f"/api/v1/suites/{sid}/column-policy",
        json={
            "identifier_column": "ORDER_ID",
            "pii_columns": ["EMAIL"],
            "require_classification": False,
        },
    )
    assert disabled.status_code == 200
    assert disabled.json()["require_classification"] is False

Let me summarise where the compliance track now stands.

## The compliance track — where it landed

| Gap | State |
|---|---|
| **G1** #431 — data-access audit trail *(the HIPAA gate)* | **Closed** — both phases, all 3 ACs |
| **G5** #435 — encryption-at-rest evidence | **Closed** — CMK deferred with verified reasons |
| **G3** #433 — authoritative classification | **Half shipped** (fail-closed mode + precedence matrix); warehouse tags still open |
| **#1318** ADR 0041 substrate · **#1319** FK `ondelete` | **Closed** |
| **G2** #432 · **G4** #434 · **G6** #1452 · tamper-evidence #1460 | Open — G2 now unblocked |

**Twelve PRs**, 48 review findings, all fixed in-PR.

## What I'd flag from this last piece

**I shipped a false safety guarantee and the review caught it.** My fail-closed mode could *loosen*: an `identifier_column` holding emails was shown in fail-closed and masked in the default mode. Worse, I had written a test named `test_fail_closed_does_not_lift_the_governance_floor` — and it **passed**, because it covered the tag path and not the `is_sensitive` interaction. A test asserting a property in its own name while the property was false, produced by the very change meant to add the guarantee.

Two more findings were the same shape as each other: a `PUT` that silently disabled the control (our own Save button would have switched it off while editing an unrelated field) and the MCP tools doing likewise. A security control that turns itself off is the worst failure available to it.

**Measuring also corrected the gap's own description.** G3 says a mis-named column "can surface unredacted" — that's *not* true of incidental columns (already default-masked) and *is* true of the **tested** column. The hole is narrower and lands exactly where the operator pointed the check. Two of my first tests asserted my assumption and failed, which is how I found out.

## Why I stopped G3 at half

The warehouse-tag half needs per-datasource introspection **verified against live warehouses**, which are stopped. Building it blind is precisely the pattern that produced #953, #520 and #1112 in this repo. #433 stays open with both halves documented.

## Two standing caveats

1. **Nothing from this track is deployed.** Two bug classes here only appear outside a test environment — a privilege that bites only non-superusers, and a commit that matters only outside a test transaction.
2. **G1 is closed on its ACs, not its full ambition** — tamper-evidence is real, unbuilt, and tracked (#1460).

**Remaining:** G2 (#432, unblocked), G4 (#434), G3's warehouse half, G6.

"""The declared residency posture — G4 / #434, GDPR Ch. V.

`GET /api/v1/admin/deployment`. Two properties matter and neither is obvious from
the happy path: an **undeclared** region must read as undeclared rather than as a
default, and the transfer list must be **enumerated** rather than derived from
whatever happens to be configured, so a vector that is switched off still appears.

Skips without TEST_DATABASE_URL.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import uuid
from collections.abc import Iterator
from typing import Any

import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from backend.app.core.auth import get_current_user
from backend.app.core.config import get_settings
from backend.app.db.models import User
from backend.app.db.session import get_db
from backend.app.main import app


@pytest.fixture
def client(db_session: Any) -> Iterator[TestClient]:
    app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = lambda: db_session
    try:
        yield TestClient(app)
    finally:
        app.dependency_overrides.clear()
        get_settings.cache_clear()


def _user(db_session: Any, role: str) -> User:
    user = User(
        aad_object_id=uuid.uuid4().hex,
        email=f"{role}-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}@example.com",
        role=role,
    )
    db_session.add(user)
    db_session.commit()
    return user


@pytest.mark.parametrize("role", ["member", "viewer"])
def test_a_non_admin_is_refused(client: TestClient, db_session: Any, role: str) -> None:
    """Gated, and asserted rather than inherited from the router decorator.

    This endpoint enumerates the deployment's outbound integrations — useful to an
    auditor and equally useful to someone deciding where to aim.
    """
    app.dependency_overrides[get_current_user] = lambda: _user(db_session, role)
    assert client.get("/api/v1/admin/deployment").status_code == 403


def test_an_undeclared_region_reads_as_undeclared(client: TestClient, monkeypatch: Any) -> None:
    """`null`, never a default.

    A guessed region on a compliance surface is worse than a blank one: an auditor
    reading "West US 2" cannot tell it was inferred, and would record a
    jurisdiction nobody ever declared.
    """
    monkeypatch.setenv("DEPLOYMENT_REGION", "")
    get_settings.cache_clear()
    body = client.get("/api/v1/admin/deployment").json()
    assert body["region"] is None


def test_a_declared_region_is_surfaced(client: TestClient, monkeypatch: Any) -> None:
    """The point of the endpoint: readable without shell access to the deployment."""
    monkeypatch.setenv("DEPLOYMENT_REGION", "westeurope")
    get_settings.cache_clear()
    body = client.get("/api/v1/admin/deployment").json()
    assert body["region"] == "westeurope"


def test_a_disabled_transfer_vector_is_still_listed(client: TestClient) -> None:
    """Enumerated, not derived.

    The LLM seam does not exist yet, and listing it as `enabled: false` is the
    point: an auditor should see that it was considered and is off, rather than
    having to infer its absence from a list that only shows what is switched on.
    A vector that appears only once someone remembers to add it is not a control.
    """
    body = client.get("/api/v1/admin/deployment").json()
    names = {t["name"] for t in body["external_transfers"]}
    assert {"alert_delivery", "llm_intelligence", "telemetry"} <= names

    llm = next(t for t in body["external_transfers"] if t["name"] == "llm_intelligence")
    assert llm["enabled"] is False
    assert len(llm["detail"]) > 40, "a vector with no explanation is a row, not a disclosure"


def test_every_transfer_vector_explains_itself(client: TestClient) -> None:
    """A name and a boolean tell an auditor nothing about what actually leaves.

    Each entry has to say what it carries and who chose the destination — for two
    of the three, the endpoint is operator-configured and its location is outside
    DataQ's knowledge, which is a fact that must be stated rather than glossed.
    """
    body = client.get("/api/v1/admin/deployment").json()
    thin = [t["name"] for t in body["external_transfers"] if len(t["detail"].strip()) < 40]
    assert not thin, f"transfer vectors with no substantive detail: {thin}"

new = """## Data residency

Where data lives, and what can take it elsewhere. GDPR Ch. V asks a controller to
answer both; this section is the answer for the reference deployments, and
`GET /api/v1/admin/deployment` is the same answer read live from a running
instance (workspace-admin only) so it can be checked rather than trusted.

**One declared jurisdiction per deployment**, set by a single IaC variable
(`azure_location` / `aws_region`) and declared to the app as `DEPLOYMENT_REGION`.
The app's value is a **declaration, not a verification** — software cannot confirm
which datacentre its database sits in — and it is reported as `null` when unset,
so an auditor sees a gap rather than a guess.

### Where each resource sits

| Resource | Region | Holds customer data? |
|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL (Azure Flexible Server / AWS RDS) | the declared region | **Yes** — suites, checks, results, and the incidental personal data in failing-row samples |
| Secret store (Key Vault / Secrets Manager / OpenBao) | the declared region | Warehouse credentials, not customer data |
| Container Apps / ECS compute | the declared region | In transit only |
| Object storage (AWS landing bucket) | the declared region | Whatever the operator lands there |
| Telemetry (App Insights / CloudWatch / OTLP) | the sink's region — **operator-chosen** | Operational metadata; PII redacted at the logger |
| CloudFront (AWS only) | **global edge** | **No.** Only fingerprinted static assets are cached (`/assets/*.<ext>`); every other path is pass-through, so no API response and no failing-row sample is stored at an edge location |
| WAFv2 Web ACL (AWS only) | **`us-east-1`, unavoidably** | **No** — the ACL is rule configuration. CloudFront-scoped ACLs exist only in `us-east-1` regardless of where the stack lives |

The last two rows are the honest exceptions, and both are stated rather than
omitted: a reviewer who finds a `us-east-1` provider alias in an `eu-west` stack
should find it explained here rather than have to work out whether it matters.

### The assertion that catches drift

The Azure stack shares a Container Apps environment, declared as a `data` source —
so its region is set by whoever created it, and **every Container App and Job in
the stack inherits it** (a Job must sit in its environment's region). Left
unchecked, moving or recreating that shared environment elsewhere would relocate
all of the app's compute with a clean `apply` and no signal.

`aca.tf` therefore carries a `postcondition` comparing the shared environment's
actual location against `var.azure_location`, so a mismatch fails the plan with a
message naming both. For a Ch. V control, "we did not notice the jurisdiction
changed" is the whole failure mode.

### What can move data out

Enumerated at `GET /api/v1/admin/deployment` — enumerated rather than derived, so
a vector that is switched **off** still appears and an auditor can see it was
considered:

- **Alert delivery** — webhooks and email carry check names, statuses and, when a
  failing sample is included, *redacted* sample values. The destination is
  operator-configured and its location is outside DataQ's knowledge.
- **Telemetry** — traces and logs to an operator-chosen sink; PII is redacted at
  the logger, so this is operational metadata rather than warehouse values.
- **LLM intelligence** — **not built.** When it lands it is a Ch. V transfer by
  construction; its intended posture (schema-only context, PII-redacted,
  local-endpoint option) is recorded in
  [post-v1-dq-intelligence-notes.md](post-v1-dq-intelligence-notes.md).

Deploying into another jurisdiction is a variable change, not a fork: the same
images and the same IaC take a different region. What DataQ does **not** do is
verify the result — that remains the deploying organization's attestation, which
is the correct split for a customer-deployed product.

## Reporting a vulnerability"""

| WAFv2 Web ACL (AWS only) | **`us-east-1`, unavoidably** | **No** — the ACL is rule configuration. CloudFront-scoped ACLs exist only in `us-east-1` regardless of where the stack lives |

The last two rows are the honest exceptions, and both are stated rather than
omitted: a reviewer who finds a `us-east-1` provider alias in an `eu-west` stack
should find it explained here rather than have to work out whether it matters.

### The assertion that catches drift

The Azure stack shares a Container Apps environment, declared as a `data` source —
so its region is set by whoever created it, and **every Container App and Job in
the stack inherits it** (a Job must sit in its environment's region). Left
unchecked, moving or recreating that shared environment elsewhere would relocate
all of the app's compute with a clean `apply` and no signal.

`aca.tf` therefore carries a `postcondition` comparing the shared environment's
actual location against `var.azure_location`, so a mismatch fails the plan with a
message naming both. For a Ch. V control, "we did not notice the jurisdiction
changed" is the whole failure mode.

### What can move data out

Enumerated at `GET /api/v1/admin/deployment` — enumerated rather than derived, so
a vector that is switched **off** still appears and an auditor can see it was
considered:

- **Alert delivery** — webhooks and email carry check names, statuses and, when a
  failing sample is included, *redacted* sample values. The destination is
  operator-configured and its location is outside DataQ's knowledge.
- **Telemetry** — traces and logs to an operator-chosen sink; PII is redacted at
  the logger, so this is operational metadata rather than warehouse values.
- **LLM intelligence** — **not built.** When it lands it is a Ch. V transfer by
  construction; its intended posture (schema-only context, PII-redacted,
  local-endpoint option) is recorded in
  [post-v1-dq-intelligence-notes.md](post-v1-dq-intelligence-notes.md).

Deploying into another jurisdiction is a variable change, not a fork: the same
images and the same IaC take a different region. What DataQ does **not** do is
verify the result — that remains the deploying organization's attestation, which
is the correct split for a customer-deployed product.

s = s.replace(anchor, new, 1)
open(p, "w").write(s)

input.command:
gh issue create --title "Residency: Azure Postgres is in West US 3 while the deployment declares West US 2" --label "security" --milestone "v1.1 Week 7 — stretch (backlog burn-down)" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Found while building G4 ([#434](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/434)) — by a `/code-review` pass that checked the **running deployment** rather than the IaC, which is the only way this was visible.

## The discrepancy

```
azure_location (declared)      : West US 2
dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd (actual)  : West US 3
```

Verified with `az postgres flexible-server list`. Every other Azure resource in the stack is in West US 2.

**This is the one resource that holds personal data** — `results.sample_failures` and list-shaped `observed_value` (#1229/#1253) — so it is the resource residency claims are *about*.

## Severity: real, but not a transfer

Both are US regions, so this is **not** a GDPR Ch. V cross-border transfer and there is no regulatory exposure today. What it is:

- a mismatch between what the deployment **declares** and where the data **sits**, and
- a claim the residency matrix in `docs/security.md` briefly made and **got wrong**. A compliance document that is false about the live deployment is worse than the gap it describes; that has been corrected in [#1464](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1464).

## Why it happened

The subscription caps PostgreSQL Flexible Servers at **one**, so the app shares the harness's server and declares it as a `data` source (`postgres.tf`). Its region was therefore fixed by whoever created it, not by `azure_location` — the same shared-resource shape that motivated the Container Apps environment assertion in the same PR.

## What #1464 already does

- States the discrepancy in the residency matrix rather than smoothing it over.
- Adds a `check` block on the Postgres data source, so it is named on **every plan** instead of being invisible. Deliberately a `check` (warns) and not a `postcondition` (blocks): a blocking assertion would fail every apply until someone moves a database, which is an operational decision the IaC should not make unilaterally.
- Keeps G4 at 🟠 rather than 🟢 in the compliance register, on exactly this basis.

## What is left to decide

Three options, and the choice is operational rather than technical:

1. **Accept and re-declare** — set `azure_location = "West US 3"` so the declaration matches reality. Cheapest, and honest, but it moves the *app* resources on the next apply, which is a real change.
2. **Accept and document as a permanent exception** — like the CloudFront/WAF rows already in the matrix. Requires no change and keeps the `check` warning as the standing signal.
3. **Move the database** — a new server plus a data migration, and it collides with the same 1-server cap that produced the shared design. Also the only option that would let a `postcondition` replace the `check`.

Worth resolving before any deployment where the declared jurisdiction carries weight; the demo estate is not one.

Refs #434, #1464, #435 (the same 1-server cap blocks CMK there).
EOF
)" 2>&1|tail -2

**Fourteen PRs**, ~60 review findings, all fixed in-PR.

**Building the residency control immediately found that the live deployment doesn't match its own declaration.** The Azure Postgres server — the only resource holding personal data — is in **West US 3** while the deployment declares **West US 2**. I verified it with `az`, after my matrix had already asserted they agreed.

The access events and retention sweep should be observed on the live stacks before G1 is treated as operationally closed.

## What shipped

| Gap | Result |
|---|---|
| **G1** #431 — data-access audit trail *(the HIPAA gate)* | **Closed** — ADR 0041 both phases; config events on all 35 mutating routes, read events on REST + MCP |

| **G3** #433 | **Half** — fail-closed mode + precedence matrix |
| **G2** #432 | Open, **now unblocked** |

Fifteen PRs, ~60 review findings, all fixed in-PR. Backend suite 4760 → green throughout.

## What the reviews caught that I'd missed

Three of these were in code my changes only *aged*, and two were live-deployment facts:

- **The Azure Postgres is in West US 3** while the deployment declares West US 2 — and my residency matrix had asserted they matched. I'd checked the IaC; the reviewer checked the running deployment. Filed as **#1465**.
- **My transfer register named the unbuilt LLM feature and omitted `/mcp`**, which serves failing samples to third-party AI clients *in production today*.
- **The access events never persisted.** `get_db` doesn't commit, so every event was rolled back — while four tests passed, because they read the row back through the same transaction that added it.
- **Fail-closed mode could *loosen*** — and I'd written a test named `..._does_not_lift_the_governance_floor` that passed while the property was false.
- **An erased author's suites would have vanished from the Admin overview** while still running on schedules.

## Honest tally on my own tests

**Sixteen regression tests passed against their own mutations and had to be rebuilt.** The recurring cause was environment blindness: the suite runs as a Postgres superuser (so `REVOKE` has no effect) and inside a shared transaction (so "did it commit?" is unanswerable). Both now have dedicated real-database harnesses.

## What I deliberately did not do

- **G3's warehouse-tag half** — needs live warehouses, which are stopped. Building driver-boundary code blind is the pattern behind #953/#520/#1112 here.
- **Resolve the West US 3 mismatch** — the fix is operational (a 1-server subscription cap forced the shared server), so I filed it with three options rather than choosing for you.
- **Deploy any of it.** Two bug classes in this track only surface outside a test environment. I'd want the access events and the retention sweep observed on the live Azure and AWS stacks before G1 is called operationally closed.

**Next**, if you want to continue: G2 (#432) is the largest remaining gap and is now unblocked.
Now let me verify the check actually passes against live Azure — otherwise I've just written a different unverified claim.

content.text:
Here's the grounded answer.

## Roughly 2–3 PRs of build, plus one blocked step and one decision for you

**The seam is already done.** `tags` is threaded through all **9** redaction call sites, the precedence ladder is tested, and fail-closed mode ships. What's missing is only the *source*.

### Build work

| Piece | Effort | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Tag store + fetch seam | ~1 PR | New table + migration; per-type impls mirroring the existing `list_columns` dispatch |
| Refresh mechanism | folded into above | The ADR-0040 **inventory sync** is the natural home — it already has the beat, per-connection error isolation and staleness signals |
| Wire into the read path | ~½ PR | Lookup keyed by the suite's asset; the call sites already accept `tags` |
| Live verification | ~½ PR | **Blocked** — see below |

### The scoping fact that changes what "closing G3" means

Only **2 of the 6** datasource types have any column-tag concept: `snowflake` and `unity_catalog` — the same two with warehouse providers. ADLS, S3, Iceberg and flat files have **no authoritative source to consume**. For those, the name/value heuristic + suite policy + fail-closed mode stay the only mechanism, permanently.

So G3 can be *closed*, but its "authoritative" claim will always be qualified by datasource. I'd want the issue's AC reworded to say so rather than closing over it.

### What's actually blocking

Live Snowflake and Databricks. Per the standing rule, tag reads are a driver-boundary question that only a live run answers — and there are two specific unknowns a live run would settle:

- **Snowflake**: `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TAG_REFERENCES_ALL_COLUMNS` needs privileges on the tag itself; `ACCOUNT_USAGE.TAG_REFERENCES` works but has **up to 2h latency**. Which is usable depends on the connection role's grants.
- **Unity Catalog**: `system.information_schema.column_tags` needs the `system` catalog enabled and granted.

Waking the harness is ~CAD 17/day for the Azure side; Snowflake is separate.

### The decision I'd want from you before building

**Tag vocabulary mapping.** Snowflake has `privacy_category`/`semantic_category`; UC tags are arbitrary key/values; our floor currently matches `sensitive|pii|confidential|restricted|secret` and clears `public|non_sensitive`. Options: honour a documented convention only, or make the mapping configurable per connection. That's a design call, not mechanical.

### The risk worth naming

**A half-working tag reader is worse than none.** Fail-closed mode treats an explicit non-sensitive tag as a *clearance* — so a fetcher that wrongly returns `public` un-masks data that would otherwise be hidden. The failure modes (no permission, stale cache, partial results) all have to fail **safe**, and that's where the care goes, not in the SQL.

def refresh_asset_column_tags(
    session: Any,
    *,
    suite: Any,
    connection: Connection,
    target: Any,
    secret_store: SecretStore,
) -> dict[str, str] | None:
    """Read the target's column tags and cache them on the suite's asset.

    Called from the run path, which is the one moment DataQ already holds the
    warehouse credentials and the resolved target. Returns the map it stored, or
    `None` when there was nothing to do.

    **Swallows every failure.** A governance lookup must never be the reason a
    data-quality run fails, and — more importantly — a fetcher that guessed on
    failure could hand fail-closed mode a false clearance. Silence degrades to
    exactly the pre-G3 behaviour, which is the only safe direction.

    A no-op when the suite has no `asset_id` (nothing to cache against) or the
    datasource has no tag concept.
    """
    if connection.type not in TAGGABLE_TYPES:
        return None
    asset_id = getattr(suite, "asset_id", None)
    if asset_id is None:
        return None

    table = getattr(target, "table", None)
    if not table:
        return None

    try:
        tags = fetch_column_tags(
            connection,
            table=str(table),
            schema=getattr(target, "schema", None),
            catalog=getattr(target, "catalog", None),
            secret_store=secret_store,
        )
        asset = session.get(Asset, asset_id)
        if asset is None:
            return None
        # Written even when EMPTY, together with the timestamp: "we looked and
        # found none" is a different fact from "we never looked", and the
        # timestamp is the only thing that distinguishes them for an operator
        # asking why a column surfaced. The redactor treats both identically.
        asset.column_tags = tags
        asset.column_tags_refreshed_at = datetime.now(UTC)
        session.commit()
        if tags:
            log.info(
                "column_tags_refreshed",
                asset_id=str(asset_id),
                tagged_columns=len(tags),
                connection_type=connection.type,
            )
        return tags
    except Exception as exc:
        try:
            session.rollback()
        except Exception:  # pragma: no cover - defensive
            pass
        log.warning(
            "column_tags_refresh_failed",
            connection_type=connection.type,
            error_type=type(exc).__name__,
        )
        return None

"""Warehouse column tags — G3 / #433.

The SQL is the least interesting part of this module and the least testable
without a warehouse; what these tests pin is the **semantics**, which is where the
danger is. This map feeds a *clearance* path in fail-closed mode, so every
ambiguity has a safe direction and a dangerous one, and each test below names
which is which.

The live half — that the queries actually run against Snowflake and Unity Catalog
— is deliberately not simulated here. A fake cursor returning the rows I expect
would prove only that I can imagine a result set; per the standing rule, it needs
a live run.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any

import pytest

from backend.app.services import column_tags as ct


# ── the documented convention ────────────────────────────────────────────────


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    ("value", "expected"),
    [
        ("sensitive", ct.SENSITIVE),
        ("pii", ct.SENSITIVE),
        ("confidential", ct.SENSITIVE),
        ("restricted", ct.SENSITIVE),
        ("secret", ct.SENSITIVE),
        ("public", ct.NON_SENSITIVE),
        ("non_sensitive", ct.NON_SENSITIVE),
        ("nonsensitive", ct.NON_SENSITIVE),
        ("  PII  ", ct.SENSITIVE),
        ("Public", ct.NON_SENSITIVE),
    ],
)
def test_the_documented_vocabulary(value: str, expected: str) -> None:
    """Case- and whitespace-insensitive, because a tag is typed by a human in a
    warehouse UI and `Public ` is the same statement as `public`."""
    assert ct.normalize_tag(ct.DATAQ_TAG_KEY, value) == expected


@pytest.mark.parametrize("value", ["internal", "restricted-ish", "level-3", "", "yes", "1"])
def test_an_unrecognised_value_is_ignored_not_guessed(value: str) -> None:
    """`None` — no opinion — so the column falls through to the suite policy and
    then the classifier, exactly as if it were untagged.

    The alternative is to guess, and guessing has only two directions: treat it as
    sensitive (mask data the operator may need, annoying but safe) or as a
    clearance (**un-mask data**, in fail-closed mode especially). Neither is worth
    the risk when "no opinion" is available and already has a well-defined
    meaning downstream.

    `internal` is in this list deliberately — it *sounds* like a classification
    and is commonly the default stamp on everything, so reading it as a clearance
    would clear whole tables.
    """
    assert ct.normalize_tag(ct.DATAQ_TAG_KEY, value) is None


def test_an_unrecognised_tag_KEY_is_ignored() -> None:
    """Only the documented key and Snowflake's own system tag are read.

    A warehouse carries many tags — cost centre, owner, retention — and reading
    an arbitrary one as a classification would let an unrelated `public` value on
    a `visibility` tag clear a column of SSNs.
    """
    assert ct.normalize_tag("cost_centre", "public") is None
    assert ct.normalize_tag("visibility", "public") is None


# ── Snowflake's own classification ───────────────────────────────────────────


@pytest.mark.parametrize("value", ["IDENTIFIER", "QUASI_IDENTIFIER", "SENSITIVE"])
def test_snowflake_privacy_category_always_masks(value: str) -> None:
    """All three of Snowflake's privacy categories denote personal data.

    Honoured in addition to the convention because the warehouse assigned it —
    it is the most authoritative signal available on that platform, and it costs
    nothing extra since the same query returns it.
    """
    assert ct.normalize_tag("PRIVACY_CATEGORY", value) == ct.SENSITIVE


def test_snowflake_privacy_category_never_clears() -> None:
    """It has no clearance side, and inventing one would be wrong.

    Snowflake omits the tag for data it does not consider personal rather than
    setting it to some "public" value — so an unexpected value means *unknown*,
    not *safe*.
    """
    assert ct.normalize_tag("PRIVACY_CATEGORY", "PUBLIC") is None
    assert ct.normalize_tag("PRIVACY_CATEGORY", "NONE") is None


# ── conflicts and shapes ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────


def test_sensitive_wins_a_contradictory_pair() -> None:
    """A column tagged both ways is a governance contradiction, and the
    resolution is not arbitrary.

    This map feeds a clearance path, so resolving toward `public` would let a
    mislabelled column surface. Masking a column someone also called public is a
    visible, recoverable annoyance; the reverse is a silent disclosure. Asserted
    in **both orders**, since a first-write-wins implementation would pass one and
    fail the other.
    """
    rows_public_first = [
        ("EMAIL", ct.DATAQ_TAG_KEY, "public"),
        ("EMAIL", ct.DATAQ_TAG_KEY, "pii"),
    ]
    rows_pii_first = list(reversed(rows_public_first))
    assert ct._rows_to_tags(rows_public_first) == {"email": ct.SENSITIVE}
    assert ct._rows_to_tags(rows_pii_first) == {"email": ct.SENSITIVE}


def test_column_names_are_lower_cased_to_match_the_redactor() -> None:
    """Snowflake returns identifiers upper-cased; the redactor matches on the
    lower-cased name. A map keyed `EMAIL` would silently match nothing — present,
    plausible, and completely inert."""
    assert ct._rows_to_tags([("EMAIL", ct.DATAQ_TAG_KEY, "pii")]) == {"email": ct.SENSITIVE}


def test_rows_with_no_recognised_tag_produce_no_entry() -> None:
    """An empty map, not an entry with a null verdict — the redactor's contract is
    "a column is in this map or it is not"."""
    assert ct._rows_to_tags([("EMAIL", "cost_centre", "finance")]) == {}


def test_a_datasource_with_no_tag_concept_returns_empty(monkeypatch: Any) -> None:
    """Only Snowflake and Unity Catalog have column tags. For ADLS, S3, Iceberg
    and flat files there is no authoritative source to read — and this must
    return `{}` without ever opening a connection, since there is nothing to ask.
    """

    class _Conn:
        type = "s3"
        config: dict[str, Any] = {}

    def _explode(*_a: Any, **_k: Any) -> Any:  # pragma: no cover - must not run
        raise AssertionError("no connection may be opened for an untaggable type")

    monkeypatch.setattr(
        "backend.app.services.profile_service._open_connection", _explode, raising=False
    )
    assert ct.fetch_column_tags(_Conn(), table="t", secret_store=object()) == {}  # type: ignore[arg-type]


def test_a_failing_lookup_is_silence_not_a_guess(monkeypatch: Any) -> None:
    """The safety property the whole module rests on.

    No permission on the tag, a missing information_schema, a dead warehouse —
    all return `{}` and log. Never raises into a run, and never invents a
    clearance. Because fail-closed mode treats an explicit non-sensitive tag as a
    clearance, a fetcher that guessed on failure could *un-mask* data; silence
    degrades to exactly the pre-G3 behaviour instead.
    """

    class _Conn:
        type = "snowflake"
        config = {"database": "ANALYTICS"}

    def _explode(*_a: Any, **_k: Any) -> Any:
        raise RuntimeError("insufficient privileges on tag")

    monkeypatch.setattr(
        "backend.app.services.profile_service._open_connection", _explode, raising=False
    )
    assert ct.fetch_column_tags(_Conn(), table="ORDERS", secret_store=object()) == {}  # type: ignore[arg-type]


def test_snowflake_binds_the_object_name_rather_than_interpolating_it() -> None:
    """The table function takes the object as a STRING argument, so it is bound.

    Asserted because the neighbouring Unity Catalog query *cannot* bind its
    catalog (an identifier prefix) and interpolates instead — so a reader
    comparing the two should see that the difference is deliberate, not an
    oversight in whichever one they read second.
    """
    stmt = ct._snowflake_query(database="ANALYTICS", schema="RETAIL", table="ORDERS")
    compiled = str(stmt)
    assert "ANALYTICS.RETAIL.ORDERS" not in compiled, "the object name must not be inlined"
    assert stmt.compile().params["obj"] == "ANALYTICS.RETAIL.ORDERS"
PYEOF

"""A warehouse tag actually masks, end to end — G3 / #433.

`test_column_tags.py` pins the fetcher's semantics and
`test_redaction_precedence.py` pins the ladder. Neither proves the two are
*connected* — that a tag cached on an asset reaches the redactor through the read
path a user actually hits. That connection is the whole feature, and it is three
hops (asset → suite → result), any of which could quietly drop the map.

Skips without TEST_DATABASE_URL.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import uuid
from collections.abc import Iterator
from typing import Any

import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from sqlalchemy import select

from backend.app.core.auth import get_current_user
from backend.app.db.models import Asset, Check, Connection, Result, Run, Suite, User
from backend.app.db.session import get_db
from backend.app.main import app


@pytest.fixture
def client(db_session: Any) -> Iterator[TestClient]:
    app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = lambda: db_session
    try:
        yield TestClient(app)
    finally:
        app.dependency_overrides.clear()


def _seed(db_session: Any, *, tags: dict[str, str] | None, column: str = "vendor_name") -> Run:
    """A run whose failing sample carries `column`, on an asset holding `tags`.

    `vendor_name` is chosen because the name heuristic clears it (an entity-
    qualified name, #1182) — so without a tag it surfaces, and any masking in
    these tests is attributable to the tag rather than to the classifier.
    """
    owner = User(aad_object_id=uuid.uuid4().hex, email=f"o-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}@example.com")
    db_session.add(owner)
    db_session.flush()
    conn = Connection(
        name=f"sf-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}",
        type="snowflake",
        env="dev",
        config={"account": "x"},
        created_by=owner.id,
    )
    db_session.add(conn)
    db_session.flush()
    asset = Asset(
        namespace=f"snowflake://acct-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:6]}",
        name="RETAIL.ORDERS",
        env="dev",
        column_tags=tags,
    )
    db_session.add(asset)
    db_session.flush()
    suite = Suite(
        name=f"s-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}",
        connection_id=conn.id,
        created_by=owner.id,
        asset_id=asset.id,
    )
    db_session.add(suite)
    db_session.flush()
    check = Check(
        suite_id=suite.id,
        name="values",
        kind="expectation",
        expectation_type="expect_column_values_to_not_be_null",
        config={"column": column},
    )
    db_session.add(check)
    run = Run(suite_id=suite.id, status="succeeded", triggered_by="manual")
    db_session.add(run)
    db_session.flush()
    db_session.add(
        Result(
            run_id=run.id,
            check_id=check.id,
            status="fail",
            sample_failures={
                "partial_unexpected_list": ["ACME LTD", "GLOBEX"],
                "unexpected_count": 2,
            },
        )
    )
    db_session.commit()
    app.dependency_overrides[get_current_user] = lambda: owner
    return run


def _sample(client: TestClient, run: Run) -> Any:
    resp = client.get(f"/api/v1/runs/{run.id}")
    assert resp.status_code == 200, resp.text
    return resp.json()["results"][0]


def test_without_a_tag_the_value_surfaces(client: TestClient, db_session: Any) -> None:
    """The precondition every other test here depends on.

    Without it, a masking assertion below would pass against a value the
    classifier was masking anyway, and the tag would be doing nothing.
    """
    run = _seed(db_session, tags=None)
    body = _sample(client, run)
    assert "ACME LTD" in str(body["sample_failures"])


def test_a_sensitive_warehouse_tag_masks_the_tested_column(
    client: TestClient, db_session: Any
) -> None:
    """The feature, end to end: the customer's own governance decides the masking.

    The tested column is the one shown *by design* — seeing the failing value is
    the point of a sample — so a tag that can mask it is a tag with real
    authority, not a hint.
    """
    run = _seed(db_session, tags={"vendor_name": "sensitive"})
    body = _sample(client, run)
    assert "ACME LTD" not in str(body["sample_failures"])
    assert body["redaction"] in {"full", "partial"}


def test_a_tag_masks_a_sample_captured_BEFORE_it_was_applied(
    client: TestClient, db_session: Any
) -> None:
    """The reason the map lives on the ASSET rather than on each result.

    A classification is a statement about the data, not about the moment it was
    read — so tagging a column today must mask samples captured yesterday. Had
    the map been frozen onto each result at write time, this read would still
    expose the value, and the governance action would have silently applied only
    to future runs.
    """
    run = _seed(db_session, tags=None)
    assert "ACME LTD" in str(_sample(client, run)["sample_failures"]), "precondition"

    suite = db_session.get(Suite, run.suite_id)
    asset = db_session.get(Asset, suite.asset_id)
    asset.column_tags = {"vendor_name": "sensitive"}
    db_session.commit()

    assert "ACME LTD" not in str(_sample(client, run)["sample_failures"])


def test_a_suite_policy_cannot_lift_a_warehouse_tag(
    client: TestClient, db_session: Any
) -> None:
    """The floor, asserted through the API rather than at the unit level.

    A tag is set by whoever governs the warehouse; naming the column as the
    suite's row locator is an application-level override. If the override won,
    the tag would be a suggestion — and the whole point of consuming warehouse
    classification is that it is not.
    """
    run = _seed(db_session, tags={"vendor_name": "sensitive"})
    suite = db_session.get(Suite, run.suite_id)
    suite.column_policy = {"identifier_column": "vendor_name", "pii_columns": []}
    db_session.commit()

    assert "ACME LTD" not in str(_sample(client, run)["sample_failures"])


def test_a_suite_with_no_asset_reads_as_no_opinion(client: TestClient, db_session: Any) -> None:
    """The degradation path, and it must be the pre-G3 behaviour rather than a
    clearance or a crash.

    A suite with no resolved asset — targetless, or an unresolvable target — has
    nowhere to read tags from. That is the same state as a warehouse whose tags we
    cannot read, which is the state most deployments are in on day one.
    """
    run = _seed(db_session, tags=None)
    suite = db_session.get(Suite, run.suite_id)
    suite.asset_id = None
    db_session.commit()

    body = _sample(client, run)
    assert "ACME LTD" in str(body["sample_failures"]), "no tags → the ladder falls through"


def test_the_mcp_read_path_honours_the_same_tag(client: TestClient, db_session: Any) -> None:
    """The sibling door. `/mcp` serves the same samples to AI clients, and a floor
    applied at one door and not the other is the shape this repo keeps
    rediscovering — here it would mean the governance tag masks in the UI and not
    in the surface that carries values furthest.
    """
    from backend.app.mcp import server as mcp_server

    run = _seed(db_session, tags={"vendor_name": "sensitive"})
    suite = db_session.get(Suite, run.suite_id)
    payload = mcp_server._run_results_payload(db_session, suite, run)
    assert "ACME LTD" not in str(payload["checks"])

anchor = "## Data residency"
new = """## Column classification from your warehouse

DataQ masks failing-row samples by default and surfaces only what it can justify
showing (#415). The strongest justification available is **your own governance**:
if a column is classified in the warehouse, DataQ reads that classification and
treats it as the floor — a suite-level setting cannot lift it.

### The convention

A **fixed, documented convention**, not a per-connection mapping. A mapping would
be more flexible and worse: every deployment would express the same idea
differently, the mapping itself would become an unreviewed security control, and a
typo in it would silently un-mask a column.

Tag your **columns** with the key **`dataq_classification`** (matched
case-insensitively):

| Value | Effect |
|---|---|
| `sensitive` · `pii` · `confidential` · `restricted` · `secret` | **Always masked.** A suite policy cannot show it |
| `public` · `non_sensitive` · `nonsensitive` | Cleared — may be shown, unless the value itself is affirmatively personal data |
| anything else | **Ignored**, exactly as if untagged — see below |

**Snowflake additionally honours its own `PRIVACY_CATEGORY`**, set by Snowflake's
built-in classification. Its values (`IDENTIFIER`, `QUASI_IDENTIFIER`,
`SENSITIVE`) all mean personal data, so all three mask. It has no clearing side:
Snowflake omits the tag for data it does not consider personal rather than marking
it public, so an unexpected value means *unknown*, not *safe*.

**An unrecognised value is ignored rather than guessed at.** Guessing has only two
directions, and one of them un-masks data. `internal` is the worked example: it
sounds like a classification and is commonly the default stamp on everything, so
reading it as a clearance would clear whole tables in exactly the organisations
careful enough to tag them.

### Where it applies

Only **Snowflake** and **Unity Catalog** have a column-tag concept. ADLS, S3,
Iceberg and flat files have no authoritative source to read, so for those the
classification remains the suite's own policy, the name/value classifier, and
fail-closed mode. This is a limit of the platforms, not a gap in the
implementation, and it is stated here so nobody plans around a guarantee that
cannot exist.

### How fresh it is

Tags are read **on each run** of a suite against that table and cached on the
asset. So a newly-classified column takes effect from the suite's next run —
including on samples captured *before* it was tagged, because a classification is
a statement about the data rather than about the moment it was read.

If the tags cannot be read — no permission on the tag, a warehouse that is down —
DataQ logs it and behaves exactly as it did before the tag existed. It never
infers a clearance from a failed lookup, because a wrong guess in that direction
un-masks data.

### Fail-closed mode

For a dataset where "unclassified" should mean "do not show", set
`require_classification` on the suite's column policy. Nothing row-level is then
surfaced unless a column is explicitly cleared — by a `public`-family tag or by
your own `identifier_column`. The classifier is not consulted at all, which is the
point: a column called `field_7` full of national ID numbers looks harmless to a
name heuristic.

It is off by default, and deliberately: a fully-masked failing row is
unactionable, so this is a trade you make for a regulated dataset rather than one
made for you.

The governance-tag floor has been threaded through every redaction call site
since #415 and populated by nothing. This populates it: DataQ now reads the
classification a customer has already applied IN THEIR WAREHOUSE and treats it as
the rung a suite policy cannot lift — on REST and MCP alike.

decision taken on this issue. A mapping would be more flexible and worse: every
deployment would express the same idea differently, the mapping would itself
become an unreviewed security control, and one typo in it would silently un-mask
a column. The convention is `dataq_classification` on the column, with the
vocabulary the redactor already speaks — plus Snowflake's own `PRIVACY_CATEGORY`,
which costs nothing extra and is assigned by the warehouse itself.

and one of them un-masks data. `internal` is the worked example — it sounds like
a classification, is commonly the default stamp on everything, and as a clearance
would clear whole tables in exactly the organisations careful enough to tag them.

about the data, not about the moment it was read, so a tag applied today must
mask samples captured yesterday. Freezing the map onto each result would have
made a governance action apply only to future runs — silently. Read at run time,
where DataQ is already connected; never at read time, which must not open a
warehouse connection.

The governance-tag floor has been threaded through every redaction call site since #415 and populated by **nothing**. This populates it: DataQ reads the classification a customer has already applied *in their warehouse* and treats it as the rung a suite policy cannot lift — on **REST and MCP** alike.

## A fixed convention, not a per-connection mapping

Per the decision on this issue. A mapping would be more flexible and worse: every deployment would express the same idea differently, the mapping would itself become an **unreviewed security control**, and one typo in it would silently un-mask a column.

`dataq_classification` on the column, using the vocabulary the redactor already speaks — plus Snowflake's own **`PRIVACY_CATEGORY`**, which costs nothing extra (same query) and is assigned by the warehouse itself.

**An unrecognised value is ignored, not guessed at.** Guessing has two directions and one of them un-masks data. `internal` is the worked example: it *sounds* like a classification, is commonly the default stamp on everything, and as a clearance would clear whole tables in exactly the organisations careful enough to tag them.

**Cached on the ASSET, not on each result.** A classification is a statement about the *data*, not about the moment it was read — so a tag applied today must mask samples captured yesterday. **Read at run time, never at read time.** The read path must not open a warehouse connection — latency, and results have to stay readable when the warehouse is down. The run is already connected with the credentials and resolved target in hand.

**Every failure is silence.** No permission on the tag, a missing `information_schema`, a dead warehouse → `{}` and a log line. Never an exception into a run, and never an inferred clearance. Only **Snowflake** and **Unity Catalog** have a column-tag concept. For ADLS, S3, Iceberg and flat files the classification remains the suite policy, the classifier and fail-closed mode. def test_a_failed_tag_read_does_not_erase_the_cached_map(db_session: Any, monkeypatch: Any) -> None:
    """The worst of the review findings, and it inverted the safety property the
    module's own docstring claimed.

    A failed fetch used to return `{}`, which the refresh wrote straight over the
    cached map — so a permission error on the tag would **un-mask columns that
    were masked a minute earlier**. "I could not look" and "I looked and there is
    nothing" have to be different answers, because only one of them is safe to
    write down.
    """
    from backend.app.services import column_tags as ct

    run = _seed(db_session, tags={"vendor_name": "sensitive"})
    suite = db_session.get(Suite, run.suite_id)
    asset = db_session.get(Asset, suite.asset_id)
    connection = db_session.get(Connection, suite.connection_id)
    # Past the TTL, so the refresh actually attempts a read.
    asset.column_tags_refreshed_at = datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(days=1)
    db_session.commit()

    monkeypatch.setattr(ct, "fetch_column_tags", lambda *a, **k: None)

    class _Target:
        table = "ORDERS"
        schema = "RETAIL"
        catalog = None

    ct.refresh_asset_column_tags(
        db_session,
        suite=suite,
        connection=connection,
        target=_Target(),
        secret_store=object(),  # type: ignore[arg-type]
    )

    db_session.expire_all()
    assert db_session.get(Asset, asset.id).column_tags == {"vendor_name": "sensitive"}

    """The other half — otherwise "never erase" becomes "never update".

    Un-tagging a column in the warehouse is a real governance action, and it has
    to take effect. This is the case that distinguishes a cautious cache from a
    write-once one.
    """
    from backend.app.services import column_tags as ct

    run = _seed(db_session, tags={"vendor_name": "sensitive"})
    suite = db_session.get(Suite, run.suite_id)
    asset = db_session.get(Asset, suite.asset_id)
    connection = db_session.get(Connection, suite.connection_id)
    asset.column_tags_refreshed_at = datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(days=1)
    db_session.commit()

    monkeypatch.setattr(ct, "fetch_column_tags", lambda *a, **k: {})

    class _Target:

        schema = "RETAIL"

    ct.refresh_asset_column_tags(

        connection=connection,

    )
