placement, or who deploys into the EU where a two-region split could straddle adequacy
boundaries, must consolidate rather than inherit this exception."""
new = """**The constraint this places on a future deployment is stated in
[docs/security.md](security.md):** an operator whose regime cares about sub-national
placement, or who deploys into the EU where a two-region split could straddle adequacy
boundaries, must consolidate rather than inherit this exception.

**The concrete regions live here and not on the published page, deliberately.**
`docs/security.md` ships to the public docs site; this file is in `exclude_docs`. DataQ is
customer-deployed, so *our* regions are a property of one demo estate that will differ for
every operator — publishing them states somebody else's posture as if it were the product's.

The stronger argument is the incident above: the matrix asserted the database sat in the
declared region, and it had not for some time. Nobody lied; the page was written once and
the infrastructure moved. A published snapshot of live infrastructure is a claim that rots
silently, so the public page now documents the **mechanism** — declare a region, the
`postcondition` blocks, the `check` warns, `shared_pg_expected_location` records an
exception — and points readers at `GET /api/v1/admin/deployment` for the **values**, read
live from their own running system. A control you can query beats a paragraph you have to
trust."""
assert old in s
open(p, "w").write(s.replace(old, new, 1))

7	- **Related:** ADR [0020](0020-history-and-audit-strategy.md) (the v1 posture this closes out), [0027](0027-suite-permission-model-workspace-admin.md) / [0033](0033-workspace-roles-rbac.md) (the grants an audit log has to record), [0034](0034-asset-entity-openlineage-identity-lineage-pull.md) (accrete-not-delete for assets/lineage; machine-written rows), [0039](0039-openbao-self-hosted-secret-backend.md) (secrets live behind the `SecretStore`, never in a DB row); issues [#310](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/310) (this decision), [#431](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/431) (G1 data-*access* audit trail — phase 2 of decision 3), [#432](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/432) (G2 erasure), [#540](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/540) / [#541](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/541) / [#753](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/753) (the delete-path FK work); the maintainers' compliance-posture register (not published)
8	
9	## 1. Context — what changed since ADR 0020
10	
11	ADR 0020 (2026-06-20) settled the v1 posture: per-entity **Type-4 snapshot tables** where config history has a concrete need (`check_versions`, then `connection_versions`), **no SCD-2**, **no soft-delete**, **cascade-delete accepted**, and a cross-entity audit log **deferred, not rejected** — "the right tool if/when *who changed this credential/share, and to what* becomes a requirement."
12	
13	That requirement has arrived, from two directions at once:
14	
15	- **Compliance.** The maintainers' posture audit names the missing audit trail **G1 (#431)** — the single hard blocker for any PHI deployment (HIPAA §164.312(b)) — and says in as many words: *revisit ADR 0020*. #431 is scheduled (v1.1 W7 stretch), so the substrate decision has to land ahead of it or #431 invents its own.
16	- **Authz surface growth.** ADR 0027 made the workspace-admin an implicit admin on **every** suite — so a suite share is now the finest-grained grant there is, and **granting or revoking one leaves no trace of any kind today** (`share_service.py:176`, `POST`/`DELETE /suites/{id}/shares`). ADR 0033 will add a stored, mutable `users.role` on top (#740–#744, **unbuilt** — there is no `users.role` column and no role-change route yet; workspace-admin is still the `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` env allowlist, changed by redeploy). ADR 0033 §7 already names a durable record of role changes as a requirement, so the substrate has to exist before that slice lands, not after.
17	
18	### Verified state of the four claims in #310 (2026-08-13, against `main`)
19	
20	| # | Claim | Verdict |
21	|---|---|---|
22	| 1 | `check_versions.check_id` is `ondelete=CASCADE`, so history dies with the check (and with its suite) | **Confirmed** — `models.py:751`; `connection_versions.connection_id` is the same (`:547`). `changed_by` is `SET NULL` on both (`:776`, `:560`), so a snapshot outlives its author but never its entity. |
23	| 2 | No general audit log | **Confirmed** — no table carries `(actor, action, before, after, ts)`. The nearest neighbours are ownership-only `created_by` columns (there is **no `updated_by` anywhere**), `incidents.acknowledged_by`/`resolved_by_user_id`, and `api_keys.last_used_at`, whose own comment reads "telemetry, not an audit ledger" (`api_key_service.py:41`). The request log line carries `method`/`path`/`status` and **no principal** (`main.py:221-260`). |
24	| 3 | All deletes are hard deletes; "a deleted connection orphans the meaning of past runs" | **Half stale.** Hard deletes confirmed — 8 `session.delete` sites, **zero** `deleted_at`/`is_deleted`/`archived` columns in `backend/app` or in any of the 47 migrations. But the connection half of the motivation was closed by #753/#541: `delete_connection` refuses with a **409** while any suite runs against the connection (`connection_service.py:915-923`) or any comparison check names it as source (`:924-936`), with a TOCTOU `IntegrityError` backstop. **A connection can no longer be deleted out from under its runs.** What remains is *suite* deletion, which cascades checks → runs → results (#540) and is irrecoverable. |
25	| 4 | No SCD Type 2 anywhere | **Confirmed.** |
26	
27	So the honest remaining scope of #310 is narrower than when it was filed: **(b)'s headline motivation has already been met by a cheaper mechanism**, and what is actually missing is the record of *deliberate acts by a principal* — which is (c).
28	
29	#310 put four options on the table: **(a)** preserve `check_versions` history past its check's deletion, **(b)** soft-delete for connections/suites so run lineage survives, **(c)** one cross-entity audit log (`actor, entity_type, entity_id, action, before, after, ts`), **(d)** full SCD Type 2. Verdicts follow, one per numbered decision.
30	
31	## 2. Decision
32	
33	### 1. (c) **Accepted.** One append-only `audit_events` table, and it is the substrate #431 fills in — not a second mechanism.
34	
35	```
36	audit_events(
37	  id, occurred_at,
38	  action_class,            -- 'config' (phase 1) | 'access' (phase 2, #431)
39	  action,                  -- 'check.update', 'share.grant', 'connection.reauth', …
40	  entity_type, entity_id,  -- NO foreign key. See below.
41	  actor_user_id → users.id ON DELETE SET NULL,
42	  actor_kind,              -- user | pat | webhook  (see below — NOT 'system')
43	  actor_label,             -- denormalized identity at time of action
44	  before JSONB, after JSONB,
45	  request_id
46	)
47	```
48	
49	**`entity_id` deliberately carries no foreign key.** An FK leaves two options, both self-defeating: cascade (the audit row dies with the entity — exactly the failure this table exists to fix) or restrict (the audit log makes deletion impossible). The in-repo precedent is `check_versions.source_connection_id`, a plain UUID with a deliberate no-FK comment (`models.py:765-768`). This is the structural property that lets one table answer what a Type-4 snapshot table **cannot**: the delete event itself.
50	
51	**`actor_kind` has no `system` value, deliberately.** A webhook is an *external* principal (the orchestrator) and a PAT is a user's, but decision 1 below rules out machine-written rows entirely — so a `system` value would have no legitimate producer and would exist purely as an invitation to smuggle routine machine writes in under it. Add it only when a config-changing act by DataQ *on its own authority* actually exists, and name that act in the same change.
52	
53	**Phase 1 (this decision, #310) is config/action events. Phase 2 (#431/G1) is data-read events, on the same table**, discriminated by `action_class` so retention, indexing and — if read volume ever demands it — physical partitioning can diverge per class without a second schema, a second authz gate, or a second redaction seam. #431 does **not** get its own table; it gets rows.
54	
55	**The two phases have opposite latency contracts, and that is deliberate.** A phase-1 event is written **inside the mutation's own transaction**: if the audit write fails, the mutation rolls back, so an applied change and its record can never diverge (fail-closed, and the change that "isn't recorded" also didn't happen). A phase-2 read event must **not** sit in a read's critical path (#431's own AC-3 forbids the regression); how it gets off the path is #431's decision, not this one.
56

## The stronger argument is our own incident

[#1465](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1465) happened exactly this way: the matrix asserted Postgres sat in the declared region, and it had not for some time. Nobody lied — the page was written once and the infrastructure moved. **A published snapshot of live infrastructure is a claim that rots silently**, and the fix is not to re-check it more often but to stop publishing it.

## What changed

The public page now documents the **mechanism** and points at the **live endpoint** for values:

- declare a region → `DEPLOYMENT_REGION`, reported `null` when unset so a gap reads as a gap
- `postcondition` on the shared Container Apps env **blocks** the plan
- `check` on a shared DB **warns**, compared against `shared_pg_expected_location`

The actual regions stay in the internal register, with the rationale for the split recorded beside them.

Pre-existing and unrelated to the above, found by `mkdocs build --strict`: `security.md` and ADR 0041 linked to `compliance-posture.md` and `post-v1-dq-intelligence-notes.md`, both excluded from the build. A published page linking to an unpublished one is a 404 for every reader. Now **zero**.

Docs-only.

Apps environment — a subscription quota, or an organisation's shared-platform
policy, are the usual reasons. Its region was then fixed by whoever created it and

Apps environment — a subscription quota, or an organisation's shared-platform
policy, are the usual reasons. Its region was then fixed by whoever created it and
is not something this stack chooses.

**The two are treated differently, on purpose.** A shared **database** in another
region is an **accepted exception rather than drift**: declare it with
`shared_pg_expected_location`, which turns "this server is somewhere else" from an
unexplained mismatch into a recorded decision.

A shared **Container Apps environment** has **no such escape hatch, deliberately** —
it is compared against `azure_location` and a mismatch fails the plan outright. The
asymmetry follows from blast radius: one out-of-region database is a single
resource you can reason about, whereas the environment's region is inherited by
*every* Container App and Job in the stack, so accepting a mismatch there silently
relocates the entire deployment. Moving the app's compute to another jurisdiction
should require changing the declaration, not setting an override."""
assert old in s
s = s.replace(old, new, 1)
open(p, "w").write(s)

# ── 2. aca.tf: remediation must point somewhere that exists ──
p = "deploy/terraform/azure/aca.tf"
s = open(p).read()
old = """        Either move the workload back, or change azure_location deliberately and
        update the residency matrix in docs/security.md."""
new = """        There is deliberately no override for this one (unlike the shared DB's
        check): the environment's region is inherited by every Container App and
        Job here, so accepting a mismatch would relocate the whole deployment.
        Either move the workload back, or change azure_location deliberately."""
assert old in s
s = s.replace(old, new, 1)
open(p, "w").write(s)

# ── 3. postgres.tf: describe the mechanism, not one deployment's regions ──
p = "deploy/terraform/azure/postgres.tf"
s = open(p).read()
old = """# THIS deployment sets the override, because the subscription's 1-server cap
# forced the app onto the harness's shared server: West US 3, while the app is in
# West US 2. That is an **accepted exception** (#1465) — same jurisdiction
# (United States), which is what GDPR Ch. V keys on — recorded in the residency
# matrix in docs/security.md alongside the CloudFront and WAF exceptions."""
new = """# Setting the override is how a deployment records an ACCEPTED EXCEPTION — most
# often because a subscription quota or a shared-platform policy forced the app
# onto a server someone else created, in a region this stack does not choose.
#
# The basis on which such an exception is acceptable is JURISDICTION, not region:

# adequacy boundary do. Record the reasoning wherever this deployment's posture
# lives; concrete regions are deliberately not written into this repo, since they

**Your instinct is backed by our own incident.** #1465 happened exactly this way — the matrix asserted Postgres sat in the declared region and it hadn't for some time. Nobody lied; the page was written once and the infrastructure moved. That's the failure mode of publishing live-infrastructure facts, and the fix isn't to re-check more often, it's to stop publishing them.

The published page now carries the **mechanism** (declare a region → `postcondition` blocks, `check` warns, `shared_pg_expected_location` records an exception) and points at `GET /api/v1/admin/deployment` for **values**, read live from the reader's own system. A control you can query beats a paragraph you have to trust.

## It went one layer deeper than docs

`postgres.tf` had `West US 3 / West US 2` hardcoded in a **tracked source comment** — the same defect, in code. Fixed; the value lives only in the gitignored tfvars, so the check still works locally.

## What I kept concrete, and why

CloudFront's global edge and the WAF's forced `us-east-1`. Those aren't our hosting — they're true of every AWS deployment, and a reviewer finding a `us-east-1` alias in an `eu-west` stack should find it explained.

## Review caught me inventing a control

I'd written that a shared **Container Apps environment** in another region can be declared via `shared_pg_expected_location`. It can't — that variable only feeds the Postgres check; the CAE postcondition has no override and hard-fails. Now stated as the deliberate asymmetry it is: one out-of-region database is a single resource; the CAE's region is inherited by *every* app and job, so accepting a mismatch there relocates the whole deployment.

Also fixed **four dead links** on the public site (published pages linking to `exclude_docs` files) — `mkdocs --strict` now reports zero.

# Build the MkDocs Material site and publish it to GitHub Pages (#288).
# Requires Pages enabled with Source = "GitHub Actions" (Settings → Pages) once.
#
# The build ALSO runs on pull requests (#834). `mkdocs build --strict` aborts on a
# warning — a broken cross-doc link is enough — and this used to run on `main` only,
# so a bad link merged green and then silently killed every publish. The site sat
# two days stale before anyone noticed. Build on the PR; publish only from `main`.
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - docs/**
      - mkdocs.yml
      - requirements-docs.txt
      - .github/workflows/docs.yml
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - docs/**
      - mkdocs.yml
      - requirements-docs.txt
      - .github/workflows/docs.yml
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

# One in-flight Pages deployment at a time; don't cancel a publish mid-flight.
concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

### Customer-managed keys (CMK) — not offered, and why

CMK is **out of scope for the current Azure reference deployment**, and this is a recorded
decision rather than an oversight. Three independent reasons, any one of which is
sufficient:

1. **CMK is creation-time-only.** Microsoft is explicit: *"You can select the mode only at
   server creation time. You can't change the mode from one to another for the lifetime of
   the server."* The only route to CMK on an existing server is restoring a backup onto a
   **new** server — so this is a data migration, not a Terraform toggle. It is also
   one-way: reverting to service-managed keys requires another restore.
   ([Limitations of CMK](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/postgresql/security/security-data-encryption#limitations-of-customer-managed-keys-cmk))
2. **Our IaC does not own the database server.** `deploy/terraform/azure/postgres.tf`
   declares it as a `data` source — the subscription caps Flexible Servers at one, so the
   app shares a server and provisions only a distinct database and least-privilege role.
   There is no `azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server` resource in that stack to attach a key
   to, and creating one collides with the same cap that produced the shared design.
3. **Our Key Vault is deliberately destroyable, which makes it the wrong key custodian.**
   It runs with purge protection **off** so a destroy/re-apply can reuse the vault name (a
   recorded decision for a demo-scoped vault). If the vault holding a CMK is deleted, the
   server goes **Inaccessible** and denies every connection. Adopting CMK therefore means
   reversing that decision — and purge protection is irreversible once enabled. Azure
   additionally requires the vault's **"days to retain deleted vaults" to be 90**, a value
   that *cannot be changed after the vault is created*: an existing vault set lower needs a
   **new vault**, not a setting change.

p = "docs/security.md"
s = open(p).read()
start = s.index("### Customer-managed keys (CMK) — not offered, and why")
end = s.index("## Column classification from your warehouse")
new = '''### Customer-managed keys (CMK)

Data at rest is encrypted with **service-managed keys** by default on both clouds.
CMK — where you hold the key — is **not wired into the IaC in this repo**, and the
reason splits into one product constraint and a set of deployment prerequisites.

**The product constraint: on Azure, CMK is creation-time-only.** Microsoft is
explicit — *"You can select the mode only at server creation time. You can't change
the mode from one to another for the lifetime of the server."* The only route to
CMK on an existing server is restoring a backup onto a **new** one, so it is a data
migration rather than a Terraform toggle, and it is one-way: reverting to
service-managed keys requires another restore.
([Limitations of CMK](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/postgresql/security/security-data-encryption#limitations-of-customer-managed-keys-cmk))

**The prerequisites, which a deployment either meets or does not:**

- **Your IaC must own the database server from creation.** A stack that attaches to
  a pre-existing server has no server resource to hang a key on.
- **The key vault must be non-destroyable.** If the vault holding a CMK is deleted,
  the server goes **Inaccessible** and denies every connection — so purge protection
  must be on, which is irreversible once enabled. Azure additionally requires
  90-day deleted-vault retention, a value that *cannot be changed after the vault is
  created*: a vault set lower needs a new vault, not a setting change.
- **You must commit to key rotation operationally.** A key that expires, is
  disabled, or becomes unreachable takes the database offline within about an hour.

Meeting all three is a deployment topology, not a feature flag — which is why CMK is
documented here rather than shipped as an option that could be enabled unsafely. A
stack that provisions its own server and a purge-protected vault can adopt it; the
maintainers' reference deployment does neither, so it is out of scope there.

'''
s = s[:start] + new + s[end:]
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("CMK section rewritten")
PYEOF

# Performance baseline — all datasources

> Captured **2026-07-10** (v1.1 W3), while both the Snowflake trial and the Azure
> subscription were still live. This supersedes the Snowflake-only W1 baseline
> (#587, kept below as the historical appendix) and is the **reference datum for
> [#595](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/595) — scale-aware
> execution (G-b)**: it measures, per datasource, where DataQ's run path stops
> scaling and *how it fails* when it does.

## TL;DR

## Appendix — Snowflake 1.2M baseline (#587, 2026-07-04, historical)

The original W1 pushdown datum, captured days before the Snowflake subscription
was to lapse (the lapse was later reversed). Environment: `DATAQ_DB.PERF`
`ORDER_LINES` 1,199,854 rows / `ORDERS_HEADER` 400,000 rows (harness generator
`PERF` tier, `--seed 587`), local stack at `v1.0.0` + #602/#603, XSMALL
warehouse, `DATAQ_READER` role.

| Measurement | Value |
|---|---|
| Test-connection (`SELECT 1`) | 3.7 s |
| Suite run, 1.2M-row table — 6 expectations + volume | 12.2 s wall, all pass |
| Suite run, 400K-row table — freshness + 2 expectations | 8.1 s wall |
| Column profiler, 4 columns on 1.2M rows | 2.6 s |
| Worker memory delta during the 1.2M run | < 50 MB (idle 1.99 GiB → peak 2.04 GiB, 14-child unpinned worker) |
| Snowflake compute, whole session | 54 SELECTs, ~2.3 s total; slowest query 1.0 s |
| Credits burned | ~0.08 |

Slowest per-query attribution (from `QUERY_HISTORY`): 647 ms unexpected-count
aggregate (uniqueness), 484 ms profiler batched aggregate, 388 ms
unexpected-values sample fetch, 213 ms profiler top-10 on the ~1.2M-distinct
column; every other expectation aggregate ≤ 15 ms, monitor scalars sub-10 ms.
Per-check `duration_ms` stays NULL in v1 by design (`run_service.py` — per-check
timing is a deferred datum). Gaps found then and since tracked: #571
(`checks_total` cosmetic 0), #605 (failure reasons — since shipped).

Reproducing the historical datum (generator `python -m mockdata backfill --tier
PERF --seed 587 --no-issues`, harness repo per ADR 0021): load via pandas
`write_pandas` with **`use_logical_type=True`** — without it, `datetime64`
columns land as epoch `NUMBER` and freshness monitors error with "not a
date/timestamp". Credits/timing were read from
`INFORMATION_SCHEMA.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY` / `QUERY_HISTORY`.

content.text:
The sweep found something bigger than the residency table.

## The real finding: two internal docs were live on the public site

**Omitting a file from mkdocs `nav` does not unpublish it.** MkDocs builds every `.md` under `docs/` and serves it by URL, indexed by search. Only `exclude_docs` unpublishes. Two files fell through:

- **`docs/ops-log.md`** — the maintainer ops journal. I confirmed it live at `https://theurgicduke771.github.io/DataQ/ops-log/` returning **200**, carrying your **personal email**, the **Postgres server name** `dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd`, Container App and RG names, CAD/day billing figures, and a **credential-expiry calendar**.
- **`docs/post-v1-assets-lineage-incidents-notes.md`** — whose two sibling design notes were already excluded; this one was simply missed.

Both are now in `exclude_docs`, with the nav-is-not-exclusion trap documented above the list.

**One honest limit: this reduces discoverability, it does not remove exposure.** The repo is **public**, so `ops-log.md` is still readable on GitHub. That's a separate decision and yours to make — CLAUDE.md mandates the file be git-tracked, so I didn't touch it. If the personal email and server name matter, the options are scrubbing those fields, or moving the file out of the repo.

## What else went

| Removed | Was |
|---|---|
| `az containerapp auth update -n dataq-app-api -g dataq-rg` | A copy-pasteable command naming *our* app — a customer running it errors, or believes those names are required |
| CMK "reasons 2 & 3" | Our subscription quota and demo vault, published as **product** limitations. A customer reads "DataQ doesn't support CMK"; the truth is "our demo vault can't host one" |
| "The Azure subscription lapsed (2026-07-12)" | Our billing status as a product caveat |
| A Snowflake trial-window note | 13 months stale on arrival |
| Warehouse names, row counts, commit SHA, "v1.1 W3" | Evidence claims survive; only the specificity that rots is gone |

## What I deliberately kept

**ADRs 0021 and 0024 keep their real resource names** — a decision record that genericizes its subject stops being evidence of what was decided. They gained a scope note saying they describe the maintainers' estate, not a product requirement. ADR 0021 now also *defines* "the harness", a word other pages used without ever introducing.

Also kept: CloudFront's edge and the WAF's forced `us-east-1` — product structure, true for every AWS deployment.

## Trim

~110 lines: a perf appendix its own header calls superseded, a footnote narrating a bug's biography where a customer needs the capability, an ADR aside about an unrelated drift bug.

**Verified against the built site, not the sources** — the email, DB hostname, CloudFront domain, Databricks workspace, Snowflake account and warehouse roles all return zero hits. `mkdocs --strict` clean, zero dead links, `tofu validate` passes.

Earlier review findings on this PR are also fixed — including one where I'd documented an escape hatch that doesn't exist (`shared_pg_expected_location` doesn't cover the Container Apps environment; its postcondition has no override).

Done with the scrub. Waiting on CI; here's the state.

## What was removed, repo-wide

Your **email**, **name as ops actor** (18×), and **Snowflake username**; the live **Postgres server**, **ADLS storage account**, **CloudFront domain**, **AWS account ID + bucket**, **Snowflake account locator**, **both Databricks workspace IDs**, and harness **ADF/RG names** in fixtures.

Replacements are **same-shaped** where the value is parsed — locator splitting, host truncation — so the tests still prove what they were written to prove rather than being weakened into anonymity.

**One was a config leak, not prose:** `shared_pg_server_name` carried your live server as a Terraform **variable default**. It's now required, with the value only in your gitignored tfvars.

## Review caught seven things, three of them mine

The honest lesson: **a blanket string replace across 40 files produces grammar bugs that grepping for the old string can never surface.** A bullet deletion that removed only its first line left a subjectless fragment on a published ADR; a substitution started mid-clause; and a published ADR still linked to `ops-log.md`, which this same PR unpublishes.

The functional one mattered more: making the variable required broke the documented `tofu apply -input=false` path, since neither the tfvars example nor the README mentioned it. Fixed, and **verified rather than assumed** — I removed the value and ran `plan`, confirming it fails fast with `No value for required variable` instead of hanging on a prompt.

Also caught: the tfvars example still hard-coded our regions three lines below `variables.tf` saying such values belong only in a deployment's own tfvars.

## Kept deliberately — tell me if you want these gone too

- **`LICENSE`'s copyright holder** — removing it breaks the MIT grant
- **`dataq-rg` / `dataq-app-*` / `dataq-cae`** — functional IaC names the stack creates and reads; removing them renames the product's resources and breaks deploys
- **`DATAQ_DB` / `dataq_retail`** in test fixtures — 30 files of churn, low value to an attacker

## The limit worth repeating

This cleans the **working tree, not git history**. Every commit carries your name and email as author metadata — inherent to git, public on GitHub regardless of file contents. A history rewrite on a public repo with 1400+ merged PRs would invalidate every SHA and cross-reference for marginal gain. For future commits, GitHub's **private-email setting** is the proportionate fix.

Verified: backend **4797 passed** (97.14%), frontend **1072 passed**, `black`/`ruff`/`tofu validate`/`tofu fmt`/`mkdocs --strict` clean, and the **built site** greps zero for every scrubbed identifier.

One incidental note: the review agent moved my HEAD to `main` mid-task (shared git worktree). Nothing was lost — the work was already pushed — but I caught it only because the files looked unchanged.

cat > scripts/check-identifiers.py <<'PYEOF'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Block personal and live-infrastructure identifiers from being committed.

This is **not** a secret scanner — betterleaks already does that, and a secret and
an identifier fail differently. A leaked secret is revoked and rotated; a leaked
identifier cannot be, because it names something real that keeps existing. The
maintainers' email, a Postgres server's hostname, a Snowflake account locator and
an AWS account id all reached this public repo and had to be scrubbed by hand
after the fact.

## What it looks for, and why these patterns

Every rule is anchored on a **provider-specific suffix or shape** rather than on a
generic word, because a generic word is where false positives come from and a hook
people learn to skip protects nothing. `\\b\\d{12}\\b` would match a byte count; an
ARN's account field will not.

Personal email is deliberately narrowed to **consumer mail providers**. Enumerating
"real-looking" domains is unbounded, but the PII actually at risk here is a
person's own address, and those live at a short list of providers.

## Placeholders pass

Documentation and tests need example values, so a match is allowed when it looks
deliberately fake — a placeholder word, an angle bracket, or a digit run that no
real allocator produces (`0000…`, `1234…`). That check is on the **matched text**,
so `acme.blob.core.windows.net` passes while a real account name does not.

Deliberate exceptions take an inline `identifier-ok:` pragma **with a reason**, on
the line or the one above it. LICENSE is exempt wholesale: removing the copyright
holder's name would break the MIT grant.

Usage: `check-identifiers.py [files...]` — no args means every tracked file.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

PRAGMA = "identifier-ok:"

# Paths where a real identifier is correct and must stay.
EXEMPT_PATHS = {
    "LICENSE",                     # copyright holder — removing it breaks the MIT grant
    "scripts/check-identifiers.py",  # this file, which necessarily contains the patterns
}
EXEMPT_PREFIXES = ("deploy/terraform/azure/terraform.tfvars",)  # gitignored real values

# Binary/vendored trees never worth scanning.
SKIP_PREFIXES = ("node_modules/", ".git/", "frontend/dist/", "site/")
SKIP_SUFFIXES = (".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".gif", ".ico", ".svg", ".pdf", ".lock", ".woff", ".woff2")

CONSUMER_MAIL = r"(?:gmail|googlemail|outlook|hotmail|live|yahoo|ymail|proton|protonmail|icloud|me|aol|gmx|zoho)\.[a-z]{2,3}"

RULES: list[tuple[str, str, str]] = [
    (
        "personal-email",
        rf"\b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@{CONSUMER_MAIL}\b",
        "a personal email address",
    ),
    (
        "azure-postgres-host",
        r"\b[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{2,62}\.postgres\.database\.azure\.com\b",
        "a live Azure PostgreSQL server hostname",
    ),
    (
        "azure-postgres-name",
        r"\b[a-z0-9-]*pg-[a-z0-9]{2,}-[a-z0-9]{5,}\b",
        "what looks like a real Azure PostgreSQL server name",
    ),
    (
        "azure-keyvault-host",
        r"\b[a-z0-9-]{3,24}\.vault\.azure\.net\b",
        "a live Key Vault hostname",
    ),
    (
        "azure-storage-host",
        r"\b[a-z0-9]{3,24}\.(?:blob|dfs|queue|table)\.core\.windows\.net\b",
        "a live Azure Storage account",
    ),
    (
        "azure-containerapp-host",
        r"\b[a-z0-9-]+\.[a-z0-9]+\.[a-z0-9]+\.azurecontainerapps\.io\b",
        "a live Container Apps ingress hostname",
    ),
    (
        "databricks-workspace",
        r"\b(?:dbc-[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}|adb-\d{10,20})\b",
        "a Databricks workspace id",
    ),
    (
        "snowflake-host",
        r"\b[a-z0-9_-]+\.snowflakecomputing\.com\b",
        "a Snowflake account hostname",
    ),
    (
        "snowflake-locator",
        r"\b[A-Z]{5,}-[A-Z]{2,}\d{4,}\b",
        "a Snowflake account locator",
    ),
    (
        "cloudfront-domain",
        r"\b[a-z0-9]{12,14}\.cloudfront\.net\b",
        "a CloudFront distribution domain",
    ),
    (
        "aws-account-id",
        r"(?:arn:aws[a-z-]*:[a-z0-9-]*:[a-z0-9-]*:|\b)(\d{12})(?::|\.dkr\.ecr)",
        "an AWS account id",
    ),
]

# A match is allowed when it is visibly a placeholder. Checked against the MATCHED
# TEXT, so this cannot whitelist a real value that merely sits on a line mentioning
# "example".
PLACEHOLDER = re.compile(
    r"example|acme|contoso|fabrikam|myaccount|mycompany|mylake|my-|your-|yourorg|"
    r"placeholder|changeme|redacted|anonymi[sz]ed|\bfake\b|dummy|sample|"
    r"\btest\b|test\d|demo|foo|bar|baz|xxx|<|\{\{|\$\{",
    re.IGNORECASE,
)
# Digit/hex runs no real allocator hands out.
SYNTHETIC_RUN = re.compile(r"(?:0000|1111|2222|1234|abcd|dead|beef|f{4})", re.IGNORECASE)


def _is_placeholder(text: str) -> bool:
    return bool(PLACEHOLDER.search(text) or SYNTHETIC_RUN.search(text))


def _tracked_files() -> list[str]:
    out = subprocess.run(["git", "ls-files"], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
    return out.stdout.split()


def _scannable(path: str) -> bool:
    if path in EXEMPT_PATHS or path.startswith(EXEMPT_PREFIXES):
        return False
    if path.startswith(SKIP_PREFIXES) or path.endswith(SKIP_SUFFIXES):
        return False
    return True


def scan(paths: list[str]) -> list[tuple[str, int, str, str, str]]:
    findings = []
    for path in paths:
        if not _scannable(path):
            continue
        p = Path(path)
        if not p.is_file():
            continue
        try:
            lines = p.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
        except (UnicodeDecodeError, OSError):
            continue  # binary or unreadable: nothing text-shaped to leak
        for i, line in enumerate(lines, 1):
            if PRAGMA in line or (i >= 2 and PRAGMA in lines[i - 2]):
                continue
            for name, pattern, why in RULES:
                for m in re.finditer(pattern, line):
                    hit = m.group(0)
                    if _is_placeholder(hit):
                        continue
                    findings.append((path, i, name, hit, why))
    return findings


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    paths = argv[1:] or _tracked_files()
    findings = scan(paths)
    if not findings:
        return 0

    print("Identifier check FAILED — these look like real, live identifiers:\n")
    for path, line, name, hit, why in findings:
        print(f"  {path}:{line}  [{name}]  {hit!r}")
        print(f"      → {why}")
    print(
        "\nThis repo is public, and an identifier cannot be rotated the way a secret can.\n"
        "Fix one of these ways:\n"
        "  • replace it with a placeholder (an <angle-bracket> name, or an acme/example value);\n"
        "  • move it to deployment-specific config that is gitignored (see\n"
        "    deploy/terraform/azure/variables.tf `shared_pg_server_name` for the pattern);\n"
        f"  • if it genuinely must stay, add `{PRAGMA} <reason>` on the line or the one above."
    )
    return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main(sys.argv))
PYEOF

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Every doc must make a deliberate publish/don't-publish choice.

**Omitting a file from mkdocs `nav` does not unpublish it.** MkDocs builds every
`.md` under `docs/` and serves it by URL, indexed by the search plugin — a page
absent from the nav is unlinked, not absent. Only `exclude_docs` keeps a file off
the site.

That is not a hypothetical. `docs/ops-log.md` and
`docs/post-v1-assets-lineage-incidents-notes.md` were both internal, both absent
from `nav`, and both live on the public site — the ops log carrying a personal
email, a live database server name and a credential-expiry calendar. Nobody
decided to publish them; the default did.

So this hook removes the default. Every `docs/**/*.md` must be in exactly one of:

  1. `nav`             — published and linked;
  2. `exclude_docs`    — not published;
  3. `PUBLISHED_UNLINKED` below — published on purpose but not in the nav, which
     today means ADRs: they are reachable from prose and from the ADR index, and
     listing forty of them in the sidebar would bury the guides.

A new file in none of the three fails, with the choice spelled out. The point is
that adding a document should require saying which of those it is.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

DOCS = Path("docs")
MKDOCS = Path("mkdocs.yml")

# Published deliberately, but not in the nav. Glob patterns, relative to docs/.
PUBLISHED_UNLINKED = ("adr/*.md",)


def _nav_entries(text: str) -> set[str]:
    """Every `*.md` mentioned in the nav block.

    Deliberately a regex over the nav section rather than a YAML parse: mkdocs.yml
    carries mkdocs-material's `!!python/name:` tags, which the safe loader refuses
    (the repo's own check-yaml hook passes `--unsafe` for the same reason).
    """
    m = re.search(r"^nav:\n(.*?)(?=^\S)", text, re.M | re.S)
    return set(re.findall(r"([A-Za-z0-9_./-]+\.md)", m.group(1))) if m else set()


def _excluded(text: str) -> set[str]:
    m = re.search(r"^exclude_docs:\s*\|\n((?:[ \t]+\S.*\n)+)", text, re.M)
    return set(m.group(1).split()) if m else set()


def main() -> int:
    if not MKDOCS.is_file():
        print("mkdocs.yml not found — run from the repo root")
        return 1
    text = MKDOCS.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    nav, excluded = _nav_entries(text), _excluded(text)

    unlinked = {p.relative_to(DOCS).as_posix()
                for pat in PUBLISHED_UNLINKED for p in DOCS.glob(pat)}

    undeclared = sorted(
        rel for p in DOCS.rglob("*.md")
        if (rel := p.relative_to(DOCS).as_posix()) not in nav
        and rel not in excluded
        and rel not in unlinked
    )
    if not undeclared:
        return 0

    print("Docs publication check FAILED — these would publish by default:\n")
    for rel in undeclared:
        print(f"  docs/{rel}")
    print(
        "\nA doc absent from `nav` is UNLINKED, not unpublished — MkDocs still builds it,\n"
        "serves it by URL and indexes it in search. Two internal documents reached the\n"
        "public site exactly this way.\n\n"
        "Decide, in mkdocs.yml:\n"
        "  • public and linked      → add it to `nav`\n"
        "  • internal               → add it to `exclude_docs`\n"
        "  • public but not in nav  → add its pattern to PUBLISHED_UNLINKED in this script,\n"
        "                             which makes that an explicit decision rather than a default"
    )
    return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
PYEOF

cd /Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ && git add -A && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
ci: add identifier and docs-publication guards (pre-commit + CI)

Two failure modes from this session, each now blocked at commit time and again in
CI — the same both-layers rule the repo already applies to secret scanning.

scripts/check-identifiers.py blocks personal and live-infrastructure identifiers.
It is deliberately NOT a second secret scanner: betterleaks already finds secrets,
and the two fail differently. A leaked secret is revoked and rotated; an
identifier names something real that keeps existing and cannot be, which is why
the values scrubbed in this PR had to be found by hand after the fact.

Every rule anchors on a provider-specific suffix or shape rather than a generic
word, because generic words are where false positives come from and a hook people
learn to skip protects nothing. Personal email is narrowed to consumer mail
providers: enumerating "real-looking" domains is unbounded, while the PII actually
at risk lives at a short list. Placeholders pass by matching the MATCHED TEXT, so
"acme.blob.core.windows.net" clears while a real account does not, and a line that
merely mentions "example" cannot launder a real value. Deliberate exceptions take
an `identifier-ok: <reason>` pragma; LICENSE is exempt wholesale, since removing
the copyright holder would break the MIT grant.

scripts/check-docs-publication.py removes the default that published two internal
documents. Omitting a file from mkdocs `nav` does not unpublish it — MkDocs builds
every .md under docs/ and serves it by URL — so each one must now be in `nav`,
`exclude_docs`, or an explicit PUBLISHED_UNLINKED list (ADRs). Adding a document
has to state which.

Both were mutation-checked rather than assumed, per the standing rule: fed the 14
real identifiers this session scrubbed (all caught) and 12 placeholders that must
keep passing (all clear), and run against a reconstructed pre-fix mkdocs.yml, where
it names ops-log.md and the assets-lineage notes exactly. That test found a real
gap the regex read fine with: the Container Apps pattern assumed three labels, and
a live ingress FQDN has four with hyphens.

Wired into the EXISTING required "Secret scanning (betterleaks)" job rather than a
new one: a new job would not be in the main ruleset's required checks, so it could
fail without blocking a merge. The job name is left alone for the same reason —
renaming it would silently un-gate the branch.

The end-of-file-fixer also normalised eight fixture JSONs on the --all-files run;
verified newline-only by hashing the content with newlines stripped.

CONTRIBUTING rules 15a/15b document both.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

content.text:
Two guards shipped, both proven against the data that actually leaked.

## 1. `scripts/check-identifiers.py` — blocks the identifiers

Deliberately **not** a second secret scanner. betterleaks already finds secrets, and the two fail differently: **a leaked secret is revoked and rotated; an identifier names something real that keeps existing.** That's why this session's values had to be found by hand after the fact.

Covers personal emails, Azure Postgres/Key Vault/Storage/Container Apps hostnames, Databricks workspace IDs, Snowflake locators and hosts, CloudFront domains, AWS account IDs.

**Design choices that decide whether it survives contact:**

- Every rule anchors on a **provider-specific suffix or shape**, never a generic word — `\b\d{12}\b` matches a byte count, an ARN's account field doesn't. A hook people learn to skip protects nothing.
- Personal email is narrowed to **consumer mail providers**. Enumerating "real-looking" domains is unbounded; the PII actually at risk lives at a short list.
- Placeholders pass by matching the **matched text**, not the line — so `acme.blob.core.windows.net` clears while a real account doesn't, and a line merely *mentioning* "example" can't launder a real value.
- Escape hatch: `identifier-ok: <reason>`. `LICENSE` is exempt outright.

## 2. `scripts/check-docs-publication.py` — closes the publishing default

Every `docs/**/*.md` must be in `nav`, `exclude_docs`, or an explicit `PUBLISHED_UNLINKED` list (ADRs). **Adding a doc now requires saying which.** Nobody decided to publish the ops log — the default did.

## Both mutation-checked, and it mattered

Per the standing rule, I proved they **fail on the real data** rather than trusting a green run:

- **14/14** real identifiers from this session caught; **12/12** placeholders still pass
- Against a reconstructed pre-fix `mkdocs.yml`, the docs guard names `ops-log.md` and the assets-lineage notes **exactly**

That test found a genuine gap the regex read fine with: **the Container Apps pattern assumed three labels**, and a real ingress FQDN has four, with hyphens. A clean run on a clean repo would have hidden it — the hook would have passed because it detected nothing.

## Enforcement point — the part worth flagging

I put both in the **existing required `Secret scanning (betterleaks)` job**, not a new one. A new job **wouldn't be in the `main` ruleset's 12 required checks**, so it could fail without blocking a merge. Same reason the job keeps its name: renaming it would silently un-gate the branch.

Pre-commit **and** CI, because pre-commit is skippable with `--no-verify`, absent for GitHub web edits, and bypassed by Dependabot — which is exactly how the typecheck-deps drift got in before.

Fittingly, **the hooks' first catch was their own scripts** (line length, an unused import, a bare `git` executable). Full pre-commit suite green, `ruff` clean, lineage/orchestration tests 379 passed, `mkdocs --strict` clean. Documented as CONTRIBUTING rules 15a/15b.

One thing they can't do: **neither guard sees git history.** They stop new leaks; the already-committed values remain reachable via `git log -S`, and commit metadata still carries your name and email. That remains the separate call I flagged earlier.

content.text:
**#1472 is merged.** Both guards are live on `main` and proven working, not just passing.

## CI verified properly

15 success, 1 skipped — and I checked the **step level**, not just the job result: `No personal or live-infrastructure identifiers` and `Every doc declares published or not` both ran and passed, on the tip commit `9a3bf083`. A green job would look identical if the steps had never executed.

## Live proof on main

A green run only proves the guard *didn't fire*. So I planted the real leaked values on `main`:

```
docs/_leak_probe.md:1  [personal-email]        'royarijit04@outlook.com'
docs/_leak_probe.md:1  [azure-postgres-host]   'dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd.postgres.database.azure.com'
docs/_leak_probe.md:1  [azure-postgres-name]   'dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd'
```

Blocked, with three independent rules catching it. The docs guard simultaneously refused the file for not declaring published-or-not. Probe removed, tree clean.

## What landed

- **`ops-log.md` and the assets-lineage notes** off the public site — the ops log was serving a personal email, a live DB server name and a credential-expiry calendar at a 200
- **Identifiers scrubbed repo-wide**, with same-shaped replacements so tests still prove what they were written to prove
- **`shared_pg_server_name`** no longer defaults to your live server — required, value in gitignored tfvars
- **Published docs carry principles, not our deployment's facts**
- **Two guards** in pre-commit *and* the required CI job, both mutation-checked
- ~110 lines of superseded archaeology trimmed; 4 dead public-site links fixed

## Before I resolved anything

I verified all 10 review threads were genuinely fixed in the tree first — including the two where the correct evidence is an *absence* (the orphaned ADR fragment and the `ops-log.md` link, both grepping `0`). Resolving without checking would have been closing my own findings on my own say-so.

## Still open, and yours to decide

**Git history.** The guards stop new leaks; they can't touch what's already committed. Old values remain reachable via `git log -S`, and commit metadata carries your name and email regardless. A rewrite on a public repo with 1400+ merged PRs would invalidate every SHA and cross-reference — I'd advise against it. For future commits, GitHub's **private-email setting** is the proportionate fix.

**Also unchanged from earlier:** nothing from the compliance track is deployed, and **G2 (#432)** is the largest remaining gap.

Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

═══════════ #431 ═══════════
TITLE: Compliance G1: data-access audit trail (who read which result/sample) — HIPAA §164.312(b)
LABELS: enhancement,security,priority/P1
MILESTONE: v1.1 Week 7 — stretch (backlog burn-down)

From the compliance-posture audit ([docs/compliance-posture.md](../blob/main/docs/compliance-posture.md), G1). **The one hard blocker for any PHI/HIPAA customer.**

**Requirement:** HIPAA §164.312(b) audit controls require a durable record of *who accessed which PHI*. GDPR accountability (Art 5(2)/30) wants processing records too.

**Current state:** we have config-*change* history (ADR 0020 Type-4 snapshot tables), but **no record of data reads** — and PII is deliberately redacted from logs, so logs can't serve as the audit trail. ADR 0020 explicitly deferred the cross-entity audit log.

**Target:** append-only access-audit log (actor, action, suite/run/result id, timestamp, request_id) covering result/sample reads + share grants; tamper-evident; its own retention policy. Revisit ADR 0020.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Read access to results/failing samples is audit-logged (who, what, when) covering REST AND MCP
- [ ] Workspace-admin can query the audit trail; retention policy documented
- [ ] Write path adds no measurable latency regression (documented check)

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

--- COMMENTS (2) ---
[TheurgicDuke771] **Scope note (from ADR 0027 / #482):** the new suite-permission model makes the **workspace-admin an implicit admin on every suite** with **workspace-wide visibility** — i.e. a workspace-admin can read *every* suite'\''s runs/results, including `sample_failures` (the incidental PII/PHI store). The access-audit log designed here must therefore capture **workspace-admin cross-suite result/sample reads** (actor, suite/run/result, timestamp, request_id), not just owner/shared reads. This widens the read surface G1 has to cover; it doesn'\''t change *what* is stored or surfaced (redaction/retention unchanged). For PHI, #431 remains the hard gate — and #482 raises the importance of closing it before broad workspace-admin is granted.

[TheurgicDuke771] **Scope note — do not build a second table.** This issue's AC ("append-only access-audit log … Revisit ADR 0020") is being answered by ADR 0041, proposed in #1321: the ADR revisits ADR 0020, **accepts** the cross-entity audit log, and makes **G1/#431 phase 2 of the same table**, not a parallel mechanism.

What that means for this issue, if #1321 merges:

- The substrate — `audit_events(id, occurred_at, action_class, action, entity_type, entity_id, actor_user_id, actor_kind, actor_label, before, after, request_id)` — lands under #1318. This issue adds **rows with `action_class='access'`**, plus the read-path plumbing and its own retention policy.
- **The latency contract is deliberately different from phase 1 and is this issue's call.** Phase-1 config events are written *inside the mutation's own transaction* (fail-closed, so an applied change and its record cannot diverge). A read event must **not** take that contract — AC-3 here forbids the regression — so how it gets off the read critical path is decided in this issue, not in #1318.
- `action_class` is what lets read and config events share one table while retention, indexing and (if read volume ever demands it) physical partitioning diverge — without a second authz gate, a second redaction seam, a second admin query surface, or a `UNION` behind "everything that happened to this suite".
- **Tamper-evidence (hash-chaining) is deliberately left here**, not in #1318 — it is only meaningful with an external anchor. #1318 ships the 90% available today: `REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON audit_events FROM dataq_app`, free because the app already runs as a least-privilege role.
- **Redaction rule that carries over (ADR 0041 §2.6):** a read event records **which** result/sample was read, never **what** it contained. Copying `sample_failures` or `observed_value` into an append-only table with a longer retention would silently defeat the #1253 purge and the #432 erasure path.
- The ADR-0027/#482 scope widening this issue already notes (workspace-admin cross-suite reads) is unchanged and still in scope here.

═══════════ #432 ═══════════
TITLE: Compliance G2: data-subject-rights machinery (erasure / access / portability) — GDPR Art 15/17/20, CCPA
LABELS: enhancement,security,priority/P2
MILESTONE: v1.1 Week 7 — stretch (backlog burn-down)

From the compliance-posture audit (G2).

**Requirement:** GDPR Art 15 (access), 17 (erasure), 20 (portability); CCPA/CPRA know/delete.

**Current state:** cascade-delete of entities + the retention purge exist, but no **targeted 'erase/export all personal data relating to subject X'** capability. Between runs, `results.sample_failures` is a real (time-bounded) residual store of subject rows.

**Target:** (a) on-demand erase of matching sample rows (not just on the retention clock); (b) structured export of stored personal data for a subject. Document that the controller's warehouse data remains their responsibility.

## Acceptance criteria

TITLE: Compliance G3: authoritative PII/PHI classification (warehouse tags over name heuristic)

From the compliance-posture audit (G3).

**Requirement:** GDPR special-category (Art 9) / HIPAA PHI must not leak via the **surfacing** path. `redact_sample_failures` surfaces the tested column when not flagged PII — but flagging is a **name-token heuristic + optional suite policy**, so a mis-named column (`field_7` holding SSNs) can surface unredacted (false negative).

**Target:** make classification authoritative — consume warehouse-native classification/tags (Snowflake/UC column tags) as source of truth, fall back to suite policy, treat the name heuristic as last resort. Optional fail-closed mode (surface nothing unless explicitly classified non-sensitive). Relates to the #415 redaction work.

## Acceptance criteria

From the compliance-posture audit (G4).

**Requirement:** GDPR Ch. V — EU personal data must stay in-region; cross-border transfer needs a lawful basis. The post-v1 LLM call is a new transfer vector.

**Current state:** deploy is region-pinned to **US (westus3)**; the seam *allows* an EU deploy but nothing documents/enforces jurisdiction; the LLM-transfer mitigation is design-only ([post-v1-dq-intelligence-notes.md](../blob/main/docs/post-v1-dq-intelligence-notes.md)).

--- COMMENTS (0) ---

═══════════ #435 ═══════════
TITLE: Compliance G5: assert encryption-at-rest in IaC + offer customer-managed keys (CMK)
LABELS: enhancement,security,priority/P3
MILESTONE: v1.1 Week 7 — stretch (backlog burn-down)

From the compliance-posture audit (G5).

**Requirement:** GDPR Art 32 / HIPAA §164.312(a)(2)(iv) addressable encryption.

**Current state:** satisfied by Azure platform-managed keys (default), but our Terraform neither asserts it nor offers CMK, and it's undocumented (no evidence for a customer security review).

**Target:** assert at-rest encryption in IaC, document it, and offer a CMK (customer-managed key in Key Vault) toggle for customers requiring key custody.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Encryption-at-rest asserted in whatever IaC exists at build time; CMK option designed/documented (build blocked while no cloud target)

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

--- COMMENTS (1) ---
[TheurgicDuke771] Checked 2026-07-27. **The stated premise is stale, but the issue is still blocked — for a different and harder reason.** Not implementing; recording the findings so the AC can be corrected.

## The AC premise no longer holds

> _(build blocked while no cloud target)_

There has been a cloud target since 2026-06-28: `deploy/terraform/azure/` is applied and running. So that half of the blocker is gone.

## The real blocker: the database is not in our IaC, and CMK is creation-time-only

Two independent findings, either of which is sufficient:

**1. DataQ's Terraform does not own the Postgres server.** [`postgres.tf`](deploy/terraform/azure/postgres.tf) declares it as a `data "azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server" "shared"` — the subscription caps Flexible Servers at 1, so the app shares the harness's server and only provisions a distinct `dataq` database + least-privilege role out-of-band. There is no `azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server` resource in this stack to assert encryption on, or to attach a key to.

**2. CMK cannot be enabled on an existing server, at all.** Microsoft is explicit ([data encryption at rest](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/postgresql/security/security-data-encryption)):

> You can select the mode only at server creation time. You can't change the mode from one to another for the lifetime of the server.

The only route is [restoring a backup onto a new server](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/postgresql/security/security-configure-data-encryption#configure-data-encryption-with-customer-managed-key-on-existing-servers) and choosing CMK there. So CMK is not a Terraform toggle on what we run — it is **a new server plus a data migration**, and it collides with the 1-server subscription cap that produced the shared-server design in the first place.

## And a conflict with a decision already taken

Our Key Vault deliberately runs `key_vault_purge_protection = false` so a destroy/re-apply can reuse the vault name (recorded in [`deploy/README.md`](deploy/README.md), and re-affirmed at the W7 externals close as "left off — demo-scoped vault"). Per the same docs, if the vault holding the key is **deleted**, the server goes `Inaccessible` and denies all connections. A deliberately-destroyable vault is therefore the wrong place to hold a CMK; adopting CMK means reversing that decision (and purge protection is irreversible once enabled).

## What is actually true today, and what is cheap

**Encryption at rest is already satisfied, unconditionally:**

> Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server always encrypts all data at rest. This data includes all system and user databases, server logs, write-ahead log segments, and backups.

Service-managed keys are the default and require no action. The same is true of Key Vault, Log Analytics and App Insights — the other stateful resources this stack owns — where at-rest encryption is platform-default and not expressible as a Terraform assertion.

So the **documentation half of this issue is the whole cheap half, and it is the half that was actually asked for**: the original wording is "satisfied … but our Terraform neither asserts it nor offers CMK, **and it's undocumented (no evidence for a customer security review)". Writing that evidence down costs little and discharges the GDPR Art 32 / HIPAA §164.312(a)(2)(iv) ask for a reviewer.

## Suggested AC rewrite

- [ ] Document the at-rest encryption posture per resource (what encrypts what, with which key, and the citation) — the customer-security-review artifact
- [ ] Record that CMK is **creation-time-only** and therefore out of scope for the current shared server; note the two prerequisites it would impose (a dedicated Flexible Server, and a purge-protected vault, reversing the recorded decision)
- [ ] Revisit only if a customer requires key custody, or when #505 (AWS/GCP IaC) creates a stack that owns its own database

Leaving open and in `v1.1 Week 7 — stretch`, retitled in effect from "assert + offer CMK" to "document the posture; CMK deferred with reasons".
